For no one knows his time. Like fish caught in a cruel net, and like birds caught in the snare, so the children of humankind are ensnared at an evil time, when it falls upon them suddenly.
This too I have seen as wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me:
There was a small city, with few men in it; and a great king came against it and surrounded it, and built great siege works against it.
And there was found in it a poor wise man, and he delivered the city by his wisdom; yet no one remembered that poor man.
And I said, "Wisdom is better than strength," yet the wisdom of the poor is despised, and his words are not listened to.
The words of the wise, spoken in quietness, are heard more than the cry of a ruler among dullards.
Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.

ecclesiastes_10.t: Dead flies make the perfumer's oil stink and ferment; so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honour.
The heart of the wise inclines to his right, but the heart of a dullard to his left.
And even on the road, when a fool walks, his sense is lacking, and he tells everyone that he is a fool.
If the ruler's temper rises against you, do not leave your place, for calmness lays great offences to rest.
There is an evil I have seen under the sun, like an error that proceeds from a ruler:
Folly is set in many high places, while the rich sit in a low place.
I have seen slaves on horses, and princes walking on the ground like slaves.
Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and whoever breaks through a wall will be bitten by a snake.
Whoever quarries stones will be hurt by them; whoever splits logs will be endangered by them.
If the iron is blunt and its edge has not been sharpened, then more strength must be exerted; but wisdom has the advantage of bringing success.
If the snake bites before it is charmed, there is no profit for the charmer.
The words of the wise man's mouth win favour, but a dullard's lips swallow him up.
The beginning of the words of his mouth is folly, and the end of his talk is evil madness.
And the fool multiplies words. No one knows what will be, and who can tell him what will be after him?
The toil of dullards wearies them, for they do not know the way to town.
Woe to you, land, whose king is a youth and whose princes feast in the morning!
How blessed are you, land, whose king is of noble birth, and whose princes eat at the proper time, for strength and not for drunkenness!
Through laziness the roof-beams sag, and through idle hands the house leaks.
Bread is made for laughter, and wine gladdens life, and money answers everything.
Even in your thought do not curse a king, and in your bedchamber do not curse a rich person; for a bird of the heavens will carry the sound, and a winged creature will report the matter.

ecclesiastes_11.t: Send your bread out upon the face of the waters, for after many days you will find it.
Give a portion to seven, and also to eight, for you do not know what calamity will come on the earth.
If the clouds are full of rain, they empty it on the earth; and whether a tree falls to the south or to the north, where the tree falls, there it will lie.
Whoever watches the wind will not sow, and whoever looks at the clouds will not reap.
As you do not know what the way of the wind is, or how bones form in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the work of God, who makes everything.
In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand rest, for you do not know which will succeed, this or that, or whether both alike will be good.
And the light is sweet, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun.
For if a person lives many years, let him rejoice in all of them, but let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many. All that comes is vanity.

Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart make you glad in the days of your young manhood; walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes; but know that for all these things God will bring you into judgement.
So remove vexation from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh, for youth and the dawn of life are vanity.

ecclesiastes_12.t: And remember your Creator in the days of your young manhood, before the days of evil come and the years arrive of which you will say, "I have no pleasure in them";
before the sun and the light and the moon and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain;
in the day when the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men are bowed, and the grinding women cease because they are few, and those who look through the windows grow dim;
and the doors onto the street are shut, when the sound of the grinding is low, and one rises at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song are brought low;

also they are afraid of what is high, and terrors are in the way; and the almond tree blossoms, and the grasshopper drags itself along, and the caper-berry fails; for a person is going to his everlasting house, and the mourners go about in the street;
before the silver cord is snapped, and the golden bowl is crushed, and the jar is broken at the spring, and the wheel is crushed at the well;
and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.
Vanity of vanities, said the Qoheleth; everything is vanity.
And besides being wise himself, Qoheleth went on teaching the people knowledge; he weighed and searched out and arranged in order many proverbs.
Qoheleth sought to find pleasing words, and what was written was upright — words of truth.
The words of the wise are like goads, and like firmly fixed nails are the collected sayings; they are given by one Shepherd.
And beyond these, my son, be warned: of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
The end of the matter; everything has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of a person.
For God will bring every deed into judgement, including every hidden thing, whether good or evil.

esther_1.t: In the days of Ahasuerus — the Ahasuerus who reigned from India to Cush, over a hundred and twenty-seven provinces —
in those days, when King Ahasuerus was seated on his royal throne in Susa the citadel,
in the third year of his reign he gave a feast for all his officials and his servants — the army of Persia and Media, the nobles and the provincial officials being before him —
when he displayed the wealth of the splendour of his kingdom and the honour of the glory of his greatness, for many days — a hundred and eighty days.

When these days were completed, the king gave a feast lasting seven days for all the people present in Susa the citadel, from the greatest to the least, in the court of the garden of the king's pavilion.

There were hangings of white cloth, cotton and violet, fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to rods of silver and pillars of marble; couches of gold and silver stood on a pavement of porphyry and marble, mother-of-pearl and precious stones.
Drinks were served in vessels of gold, and the vessels differed one from another, and royal wine was plentiful, as the king could afford.
And the drinking was by law: no one was compelled; for the king had instructed every steward of his household to do as each man pleased.
Queen Vashti also gave a feast for the women in the royal house that belonged to King Ahasuerus.

On the seventh day, when the king's heart was merry with wine, he said to Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha and Abagtha, Zethar and Carcas, the seven eunuchs who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus,
to bring Queen Vashti before the king wearing the royal crown, to show the peoples and the officials her beauty — for she was good to look at.
But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's word, delivered by the eunuchs. And the king became very angry, and his rage burned within him.
Then the king said to the wise men who knew the times — for this was the king's way before all who knew law and judgement —
and those closest to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena and Memucan, the seven officials of Persia and Media who had access to the king and sat first in the kingdom —
"According to the law, what is to be done with Queen Vashti, because she did not carry out the command of King Ahasuerus delivered by the eunuchs?"

And Memucan said before the king and the officials, "Queen Vashti has done wrong not against the king alone, but against all the officials and against all the peoples in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus.

"For the queen's affair will go out to all the women, making their husbands despicable in their eyes, when they say, 'King Ahasuerus ordered Queen Vashti to be brought before him, and she did not come.'
"This very day the noble ladies of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen's affair will say the same to all the king's officials — and there will be contempt and anger enough.

"If it pleases the king, let a royal word go out from him and be written among the laws of Persia and Media, so that it cannot be revoked: that Vashti shall not come before King Ahasuerus; and let the king give her royal position to another woman better than she.
"And the king's decree, which he will issue, will be heard throughout his kingdom — for it is vast — and all the women will give honour to their husbands, from the greatest to the least."
The proposal was good in the eyes of the king and the officials, and the king did as Memucan had said.

And he sent letters to all the king's provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, that every man should be master in his own house and speak in the language of his own people.

esther_2.t: After these things, when King Ahasuerus's rage had subsided, he remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what had been decreed against her.
Then the king's young men who served him said, "Let beautiful young virgins be sought for the king,

"and let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, and let them gather every beautiful young virgin to Susa the citadel, to the house of the women, into the charge of Hegai the king's eunuch, keeper of the women; and let their ointments be given them.
"And the young woman who pleases the king shall reign in place of Vashti." The proposal was good in the eyes of the king, and he did so.
There was a Jewish man in Susa the citadel whose name was Mordecai son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite,
who had been taken into exile from Jerusalem with the exiles taken away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried into exile.

He was bringing up Hadassah — that is, Esther — his uncle's daughter, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman was beautiful of form and good to look at; and when her father and mother died, Mordecai took her to himself as a daughter.

And when the king's word and his law were heard, and many young women were gathered to Susa the citadel into Hegai's charge, Esther was taken to the king's house, into the charge of Hegai, keeper of the women.

The young woman was good in his eyes and won his loyalty, and he hurried to give her her ointments and her portions, and the seven chosen young women to be given her from the king's house; and he moved her and her young women to the best place in the house of the women.
Esther had not told her people or her kindred, for Mordecai had commanded her not to tell.
And every single day Mordecai walked back and forth in front of the court of the house of the women, to learn how Esther was and what was being done with her.

Now when the turn of each young woman came to go in to King Ahasuerus, at the end of the twelve months prescribed for the women — for that was how the days of their ointments were completed: six months with oil of myrrh and six months with balsam oils and the ointments of the women —
then in this way the young woman would go in to the king: anything she asked for was given her to take with her from the house of the women to the king's house.

In the evening she would go in, and in the morning she would return to the second house of the women, into the charge of Shaashgaz the king's eunuch, keeper of the concubines. She would not go in to the king again unless the king delighted in her and she was summoned by name.

And when the turn came for Esther, the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai — who had taken her to himself as a daughter — to go in to the king, she asked for nothing except what Hegai the king's eunuch, keeper of the women, advised. And Esther won favour in the eyes of all who saw her.
And Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus, to his royal house, in the tenth month — that is, the month of Tebeth — in the seventh year of his reign.
And the king loved Esther more than all the women, and she won favour and loyalty before him more than all the virgins; and he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen in place of Vashti.
And the king gave a great feast for all his officials and his servants — Esther's feast — and he granted a remission to the provinces and gave gifts with royal liberality.
And when virgins were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate.
Esther still did not tell her kindred or her people, just as Mordecai had commanded her; and Esther did what Mordecai said, just as when she was under his guardianship.

In those days, while Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs from among the keepers of the threshold, became angry and sought to lay a hand on King Ahasuerus.
The matter became known to Mordecai, and he told Queen Esther, and Esther spoke to the king in Mordecai's name.
The matter was investigated and found to be so, and the two of them were hanged on a gallows; and it was recorded in the book of the events of the days, in the king's presence.

esther_3.t: After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite and exalted him, and set his seat above all the officials who were with him.
And all the king's servants who were at the king's gate knelt and bowed down to Haman, for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai would not kneel and would not bow down.
So the king's servants who were at the king's gate said to Mordecai, "Why are you transgressing the king's commandment?"
And when they spoke to him day after day and he did not listen to them, they told Haman, to see whether Mordecai's words would stand — for he had told them that he was a Jew.
And when Haman saw that Mordecai was not kneeling and bowing down to him, Haman was filled with rage.

But it seemed contemptible in his eyes to lay a hand on Mordecai alone, for they had told him who Mordecai's people were. So Haman sought to annihilate all the Jews in all the kingdom of Ahasuerus — the people of Mordecai.

In the first month — that is, the month of Nisan — in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast Pur (that is, the lot) before Haman, from day to day and from month to month, to the twelfth, that is the month of Adar.

And Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is a certain people scattered and separated among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws differ from those of every other people, and they do not keep the king's laws, and it is not fitting for the king to let them remain.
"If it pleases the king, let it be written that they be destroyed; and I will weigh out ten thousand talents of silver into the hands of those who do the work, to bring into the king's treasuries."
And the king took his signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the adversary of the Jews.
And the king said to Haman, "The silver is given to you, and the people too, to do with them as seems good to you."

The king's scribes were summoned in the first month, on the thirteenth day of it, and it was written, according to all that Haman commanded, to the king's satraps and to the governors over each province and to the officials of each people — each province in its own script and each people in its own language. It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's signet ring.

And letters were sent by the hand of the couriers to all the king's provinces: to annihilate, to kill and to destroy all the Jews, young and old, little children and women, in one day, on the thirteenth of the twelfth month — that is, the month of Adar — and to take their goods as plunder.
A copy of the writing was to be issued as law in every single province, published to all the peoples, so that they would be ready for that day.
The couriers went out, hurried by the king's word, and the law was issued in Susa the citadel. And the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion.

esther_4.t: When Mordecai learned all that had been done, Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the midst of the city and cried out a loud and bitter cry.
He came only as far as the front of the king's gate, for no one might enter the king's gate in sackcloth clothing.
And in every single province, wherever the king's word and his law reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, and fasting and weeping and wailing; many lay on sackcloth and ashes.
Esther's maids and her eunuchs came and told her, and the queen was greatly distressed; and she sent garments to clothe Mordecai and take his sackcloth from him, but he would not accept them.
So Esther summoned Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs whom he had appointed to attend her, and gave him orders concerning Mordecai, to learn what this was and why.
So Hathach went out to Mordecai, to the open square of the city in front of the king's gate.
And Mordecai told him all that had happened to him, and the exact sum of silver that Haman had said he would weigh out to the king's treasuries for the Jews, to destroy them.

He also gave him a copy of the writing of the law that had been issued in Susa for their annihilation, to show Esther and to tell her, and to command her to go to the king, to seek his favour and to make request before him for her people.
And Hathach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai.
Then Esther spoke to Hathach and gave him orders for Mordecai:

"All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know that for any man or woman who goes to the king in the inner court without being summoned, there is one law: to be put to death — except the one to whom the king extends the golden sceptre, and lives. And I have not been summoned to come to the king these thirty days."
And they told Mordecai the words of Esther.
And Mordecai sent back this reply to Esther: "Do not imagine in your own being that you, of all the Jews, will escape in the king's house.

"For if you keep altogether silent at this time, relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place, and you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether it was for a time like this that you have reached royalty?"
Then Esther sent back this reply to Mordecai:

"Go, gather all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me: do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my maids will fast in the same way. And then I will go to the king, which is against the law — and if I perish, I perish."
So Mordecai went away and did all that Esther had commanded him.

esther_5.t: On the third day Esther put on royal dress and stood in the inner court of the king's house, opposite the king's house; and the king was sitting on his royal throne in the royal house, opposite the entrance of the house.

And when the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won favour in his eyes, and the king extended to Esther the golden sceptre that was in his hand. Esther drew near and touched the top of the sceptre.
And the king said to her, "What is it, Queen Esther? And what is your request? Up to half the kingdom, and it shall be given you."
And Esther said, "If it pleases the king, let the king and Haman come today to the feast that I have prepared for him."
Then the king said, "Bring Haman quickly, to do what Esther has said." And the king and Haman came to the feast that Esther had prepared.
And at the feast of wine the king said to Esther, "What is your petition? It shall be given you. And what is your request? Up to half the kingdom, and it shall be done."
And Esther answered and said, "My petition and my request —

"if I have found favour in the eyes of the king, and if it pleases the king to grant my petition and to do my request — let the king and Haman come to the feast that I will prepare for them, and tomorrow I will do as the king has said."
And Haman went out that day joyful and in good spirits. But when Haman saw Mordecai at the king's gate, and he neither rose nor trembled before him, Haman was filled with rage against Mordecai.
But Haman restrained himself and went to his house, and he sent for and brought in his friends and Zeresh his wife.

And Haman recounted to them the splendour of his wealth and the multitude of his sons, and all the ways the king had promoted him, and how he had exalted him above the officials and the king's servants.
And Haman said, "What is more, Queen Esther let no one come with the king to the feast she had prepared except me; and tomorrow too I am invited by her, along with the king.
"But all this is worth nothing to me, every time I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate."

Then Zeresh his wife and all his friends said to him, "Let a gallows be made, fifty cubits high, and in the morning speak to the king, and let them hang Mordecai on it; and go with the king to the feast in good spirits." The proposal was good before Haman, and he had the gallows made.

esther_6.t: On that night the king's sleep fled, and he ordered the book of the records, the events of the days, to be brought; and they were read aloud before the king.
And it was found written that Mordecai had told about Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs from among the keepers of the threshold, who had sought to lay a hand on King Ahasuerus.
And the king said, "What honour and greatness has been done for Mordecai for this?" And the king's young men who served him said, "Nothing has been done for him."
And the king said, "Who is in the court?" Now Haman had come to the outer court of the king's house, to speak to the king about hanging Mordecai on the gallows that he had prepared for him.
And the king's young men said to him, "Haman is standing in the court." And the king said, "Let him come in."
And Haman came in, and the king said to him, "What is to be done for the man in whose honour the king delights?" And Haman said in his heart, "Whom would the king delight to honour more than me?"
And Haman said to the king, "For the man in whose honour the king delights —
"let them bring royal clothing that the king has worn, and a horse that the king has ridden, one that has had a royal crown set on its head;

"and let the clothing and the horse be handed over to one of the king's officials, the nobles, and let them clothe the man in whose honour the king delights, and mount him on the horse in the open square of the city, and proclaim before him, 'Thus it is done for the man in whose honour the king delights.'"
Then the king said to Haman, "Hurry, take the clothing and the horse as you have said, and do so for Mordecai the Jew who sits at the king's gate. Let nothing fall of all that you have said."

So Haman took the clothing and the horse, and clothed Mordecai, and mounted him on the horse in the open square of the city, and proclaimed before him, "Thus it is done for the man in whose honour the king delights."
And Mordecai returned to the king's gate; but Haman hurried to his house, mourning, with his head covered.

And Haman recounted to Zeresh his wife and to all his friends everything that had happened to him. And his wise men and Zeresh his wife said to him, "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of the offspring of the Jews, you will not prevail against him — you will surely fall before him."
They were still speaking with him when the king's eunuchs arrived, and they hurried Haman off to the feast that Esther had prepared.

esther_7.t: So the king and Haman came to drink with Queen Esther.

And on the second day too, at the feast of wine, the king said to Esther, "What is your petition, Queen Esther? It shall be given you. And what is your request? Up to half the kingdom, and it shall be done."
And Queen Esther answered and said, "If I have found favour in your eyes, O king, and if it pleases the king — let my life be given me as my petition, and my people as my request.

"For we have been sold, I and my people, to be annihilated, killed and destroyed. Had we been sold as male and female slaves, I would have kept silent — for the distress would not be worth troubling the king."
And King Ahasuerus said — he said to Queen Esther — "Who is he, and where is he, whose heart has filled him to do this?"
And Esther said, "A man, an adversary and an enemy — this evil Haman!" And Haman was terrified before the king and the queen.

And the king rose in his rage from the feast of wine and went into the garden of the pavilion; but Haman stayed to plead for his life with Queen Esther, for he saw that harm was determined against him by the king.

And the king returned from the garden of the pavilion to the house of the feast of wine, and Haman was falling on the couch that Esther was on. And the king said, "Will he even subdue the queen, with me in the house?" The word went out from the king's mouth, and they covered Haman's face.

Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs, said before the king, "What is more, the gallows that Haman made for Mordecai — who spoke good on the king's behalf — is standing at Haman's house, fifty cubits high." And the king said, "Hang him on it."
So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. And the king's rage subsided.

esther_8.t: On that day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the house of Haman, the adversary of the Jews; and Mordecai came before the king, for Esther had told what he was to her.
And the king took off his signet ring, which he had taken back from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai; and Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman.
And Esther spoke again before the king, and fell at his feet and wept, and pleaded with him to avert the evil of Haman the Agagite and the plan he had devised against the Jews.
And the king extended the golden sceptre to Esther, and Esther rose and stood before the king.

And she said, "If it pleases the king, and if I have found favour before him, and the matter seems proper to the king, and I am good in his eyes — let it be written to revoke the letters, the plan of Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, which he wrote to destroy the Jews in all the king's provinces.
"For how could I bear to look on the evil that will overtake my people? And how could I bear to look on the destruction of my kindred?"

And King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, "See, I have given Haman's house to Esther, and they have hanged him on the gallows, because he stretched out his hand against the Jews.

"And you, write concerning the Jews as seems good to you, in the name of the king, and seal it with the king's signet ring; for a writing that is written in the name of the king and sealed with the king's signet ring cannot be revoked."

So the king's scribes were summoned at that time, in the third month — that is, the month of Sivan — on the twenty-third day of it, and it was written according to all that Mordecai commanded, to the Jews and to the satraps and the governors and the officials of the provinces from India to Cush, a hundred and twenty-seven provinces — each province in its own script and each people in its own language, and to the Jews in their own script and their own language.
And he wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed it with the king's signet ring, and sent letters by the hand of the couriers on horses, riders of the royal steeds, bred from the royal mares.

In them the king permitted the Jews in every single city to assemble and to make a stand for their life: to annihilate, kill and destroy every armed force of a people or province attacking them, little children and women included, and to take their goods as plunder —
on one day, in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus: the thirteenth of the twelfth month, that is, the month of Adar.
A copy of the writing was to be issued as law in every single province, published to all the peoples, and the Jews were to be ready for that day, to avenge themselves on their enemies.
The couriers, riders of the royal steeds, went out hastened and hurried by the king's word; and the law was issued in Susa the citadel.

And Mordecai went out from the king's presence in royal clothing of violet and white, with a great crown of gold and a robe of fine linen and purple; and the city of Susa shouted for joy and rejoiced.
For the Jews there was light and gladness and joy and honour.

And in every single province and every single city, wherever the king's word and his law reached, there was gladness and joy for the Jews, a feast and a holiday; and many from the peoples of the land became Jews, for dread of the Jews had fallen on them.

esther_9.t: And in the twelfth month — that is, the month of Adar — on the thirteenth day of it, when the king's word and his law drew near to be carried out, on the day when the enemies of the Jews had hoped to master them — and it was reversed: the Jews themselves mastered those who hated them —

the Jews assembled in their cities, in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, to lay a hand on those who sought their harm; and no one stood before them, for dread of them had fallen on all the peoples.
And all the officials of the provinces, and the satraps and the governors and those who did the king's work, supported the Jews, for dread of Mordecai had fallen on them.
For Mordecai was great in the king's house, and the report of him went out into all the provinces; for the man Mordecai went on growing greater.
And the Jews struck down all their enemies with a striking of sword and slaughter and destruction, and did to those who hated them as they pleased.
And in Susa the citadel the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men.
and Parshandatha and Dalphon and Aspatha
and Poratha and Adalia and Aridatha
and Parmashta and Arisai and Aridai and Vaizatha —
the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the adversary of the Jews — these they killed; but on the plunder they did not lay their hand.
On that day the number of those killed in Susa the citadel came before the king.

And the king said to Queen Esther, "In Susa the citadel the Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men and the ten sons of Haman. What have they done in the rest of the king's provinces? And what is your petition? It shall be given you. And what more is your request? It shall be done."
And Esther said, "If it pleases the king, let it be permitted tomorrow also to the Jews in Susa to act according to the law of this day; and let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows."
And the king said that it should be done so; a law was issued in Susa, and they hanged the ten sons of Haman.
And the Jews in Susa assembled on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar also, and killed three hundred men in Susa; but on the plunder they did not lay their hand.

And the rest of the Jews in the king's provinces assembled and made a stand for their life, and had rest from their enemies, and killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them; but on the plunder they did not lay their hand.
This was on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar; and they rested on the fourteenth of it and made it a day of feasting and joy.
But the Jews in Susa assembled on the thirteenth and on the fourteenth of it, and rested on the fifteenth, and made it a day of feasting and joy.

That is why the Jews of the open country, who live in the towns of the unwalled regions, observe the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day of joy and feasting, a holiday, and of sending portions to one another.
And Mordecai wrote these things down, and sent letters to all the Jews in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, near and far,
to impose on them that they should observe the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and the fifteenth day of it, in every single year,

as the days on which the Jews had rest from their enemies, and the month that was turned for them from sorrow to joy and from mourning to a holiday — to make them days of feasting and joy, of sending portions to one another and gifts to the needy.
And the Jews accepted what they had begun to do, and what Mordecai had written to them.
For Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the adversary of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur — that is, the lot — to crush them and destroy them.
But when it came before the king, he said in the letter, "Let his evil plan, which he devised against the Jews, return on his own head"; and they hanged him and his sons on the gallows.
That is why these days were called Purim, after the name of the Pur. Therefore, because of all the words of this letter, and what they had seen concerning this, and what had happened to them,

the Jews imposed and accepted upon themselves and upon their offspring and upon all who joined themselves to them, so that it should not lapse, that they would observe these two days according to their prescription and their appointed time, in every single year;

and that these days would be remembered and observed in every generation, every clan, every province and every city; and that these days of Purim would not lapse from among the Jews, and their remembrance would not cease from their offspring.
Then Queen Esther, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter of Purim.
And letters were sent to all the Jews, to the hundred and twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus — words of peace and faithfulness —

to confirm these days of Purim at their appointed times, just as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had imposed on them, and just as they had imposed on themselves and on their offspring — the matters of the fasts and their cry of distress.
And the command of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim, and it was recorded in the book.

esther_10.t: And King Ahasuerus laid a levy on the land and on the islands of the sea.

And all the work of his power and his might, and the full account of the greatness of Mordecai, to which the king raised him — are they not written in the book of the events of the days of the kings of Media and Persia?
For Mordecai the Jew was second to King Ahasuerus, and great among the Jews, and acceptable to the multitude of his brothers — seeking good for his people and speaking peace to all his offspring.

exodus_1.t: These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, each man with his household:
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah;
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin;
Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.
All the persons who came out of Jacob's loins were seventy in all; and Joseph was in Egypt.
Then Joseph died, and all his brothers, and all that generation.
But the Israelites were fruitful; they swarmed, they multiplied, they grew mighty — exceedingly so — and the land was filled with them.
Then a new king arose over Egypt, one who did not know Joseph.
He said to his people, 'Look, the people of Israel are more numerous and mightier than we are.'
'Come, let us deal wisely with them, or they will multiply, and if war breaks out they too will join those who hate us, fight against us, and go up out of the land.'
So they set overseers of labour gangs over them, to afflict them with forced labour; and they built storage cities for Pharaoh: Pithom and Rameses.
But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and the more they spread; and the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites.
So the Egyptians made the Israelites serve with harshness.
They made their lives bitter with hard labour — mortar and bricks and every kind of labour in the field. All the labour they imposed on them was imposed with harshness.
The king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives — the name of one was Shiphrah, the name of the second was Puah —
He said, 'When you act as midwife for the Hebrew women, watch at the birthstool: if it is a son, you are to kill him; if it is a daughter, she may live.'
But the midwives feared God, and they did not do as the king of Egypt had told them; they let the boys live.
So the king of Egypt summoned the midwives and said to them, 'Why have you done this? You have let the boys live.'
The midwives said to Pharaoh, 'The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women. They are vigorous: before the midwife reaches them, they have given birth.'
And God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied and grew very mighty.
And because the midwives feared God, he made households for them.
Then Pharaoh commanded all his people: 'Every son that is born you are to throw into the Nile, and every daughter you are to let live.'

exodus_2.t: A man from the house of Levi went and took a daughter of Levi as his wife.
The woman conceived and bore a son. She saw that he was good, and she hid him for three months.
When she could hide him no longer, she took a papyrus basket for him and sealed it with bitumen and pitch. She put the child in it and set it among the reeds at the bank of the Nile.
His sister stationed herself at a distance, to learn what would be done to him.
Pharaoh's daughter went down to bathe at the Nile while her attendants walked beside the river. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her maidservant, and she fetched it.
She opened it and saw the child — and there was a boy, weeping. She had compassion on him and said, 'This is one of the Hebrews' children.'
Then his sister said to Pharaoh's daughter, 'Shall I go and call a nursing woman from among the Hebrew women for you, so that she may nurse the child for you?'
Pharaoh's daughter said to her, 'Go.' So the young woman went and called the child's mother.
Pharaoh's daughter said to her, 'Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will pay your wages.' So the woman took the child and nursed him.
The child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She called his name Moses, and said, 'Because I drew him out of the water.'
In those days, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his brothers and looked on their forced labour; and he saw an Egyptian man striking a Hebrew man, one of his brothers.
He turned this way and that and saw that there was no one about; then he struck the Egyptian down and hid him in the sand.
He went out the next day, and there were two Hebrew men struggling with each other. He said to the one in the wrong, 'Why are you striking your companion?'
He said, 'Who appointed you chief and judge over us? Do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?' Then Moses was afraid, and he thought, 'So the matter is known.'
When Pharaoh heard of this matter, he sought to kill Moses; but Moses fled from Pharaoh and settled in the land of Midian, and he sat down by a well.
Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came and drew water and filled the troughs to water their father's flock.
But the shepherds came and drove them away. Moses got up and delivered them, and he watered their flock.
When they came to Reuel their father, he said, 'Why have you come back so early today?'
They said, 'An Egyptian man delivered us from the shepherds, and he even drew water for us himself and watered the flock.'
He said to his daughters, 'And where is he? Why did you leave the man behind? Call him, so that he may eat bread with us.'
Moses agreed to stay with the man, and he gave Moses his daughter Zipporah.
She bore a son, and he called his name Gershom, for he said, 'I have been a sojourner in a foreign land.'
In the course of those many days the king of Egypt died. The Israelites groaned under the labour and cried out, and their cry for help went up to God from the labour.
God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.
And God saw the Israelites, and God knew.

exodus_3.t: Moses was pasturing the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian. He drove the flock beyond the wilderness and came to the mountain of God, to Horeb.
The angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the middle of a bush. He looked, and there was the bush burning with fire — and the bush was not consumed.
Moses said, 'Let me turn aside and see this great sight: why the bush is not burning up.'
When the LORD saw that he had turned aside to look, God called to him out of the middle of the bush and said, 'Moses! Moses!' And he said, 'Here I am.'
He said, 'Do not come near. Take your sandals off your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.'
He said, 'I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.
The LORD said, 'I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their cry because of its taskmasters; indeed I know its pains.'

'So I have come down to deliver them from the hand of Egypt and to bring them up out of that land into a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey — to the place of the Canaanites and the Hittites and the Amorites and the Perizzites and the Hivites and the Jebusites.'
'And now the cry of the Israelites has come to me, and I have also seen the oppression with which the Egyptians are oppressing them.'
'And now go: I am sending you to Pharaoh. Bring my people, the Israelites, out of Egypt.'
But Moses said to God, 'Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?'
He said, 'Because I will be with you. And this is the sign for you that I have sent you: when you bring the people out of Egypt, you will serve God on this mountain.'
Then Moses said to God, 'Suppose I go to the Israelites and say to them, "The God of your fathers has sent me to you," and they say to me, "What is his name?" — what shall I say to them?'
God said to Moses, 'I AM WHO I AM.' And he said, 'This is what you are to say to the Israelites: I AM has sent me to you.'

God said further to Moses, 'This is what you are to say to the Israelites: The LORD, the God of your fathers — the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob — has sent me to you. This is my name for ever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation.'

'Go and gather the elders of Israel and say to them, "The LORD, the God of your fathers — the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — has appeared to me, saying: I have surely attended to you and to what has been done to you in Egypt."'

'And I have said: I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt to the land of the Canaanites and the Hittites and the Amorites and the Perizzites and the Hivites and the Jebusites, to a land flowing with milk and honey.'

'They will listen to your voice. Then you and the elders of Israel are to go to the king of Egypt and say to him, "The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. Now let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God."'
'But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go — not even under a strong hand.'
'So I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all my wonders that I will do in its midst; and after that he will let you go.'
'And I will give this people favour in the eyes of the Egyptians, so that when you go, you will not go empty-handed.'

'Each woman shall ask of her neighbour and of the woman sojourning in her house for articles of silver and articles of gold and clothing; and you shall put them on your sons and on your daughters, and so you shall plunder Egypt.'

exodus_4.t: Then Moses answered, 'But look — they will not believe me and will not listen to my voice; they will say, "The LORD has not appeared to you."'
The LORD said to him, 'What is that in your hand?' He said, 'A staff.'
He said, 'Throw it on the ground.' He threw it on the ground, and it became a serpent — and Moses fled from it.
The LORD said to Moses, 'Stretch out your hand and take hold of its tail.' So he stretched out his hand and took hold of it, and it became a staff in his palm.
'— so that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you.'
The LORD said to him further, 'Put your hand into your cloak.' He put his hand into his cloak and brought it out — and there was his hand, struck with scale-disease, like snow.
He said, 'Put your hand back into your cloak.' He put his hand back into his cloak and brought it out again — and it had returned to be like the rest of his flesh.
'And if they will not believe you and will not listen to the voice of the first sign, they will believe the voice of the second sign.'

'And if they will not believe even these two signs and will not listen to your voice, then take some of the water of the Nile and pour it out on the dry ground; and the water you take from the Nile will become blood on the dry ground.'
But Moses said to the LORD, 'Please, my Lord — I am not a man of words, not before now and not since you began speaking to your servant; for I am heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue.'
The LORD said to him, 'Who made a mouth for a human being? Or who makes someone mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?'
'Now go. I will be with your mouth and will teach you what you are to speak.'
But he said, 'Please, my Lord — send by the hand of whomever you will send.'

Then the LORD's anger burned against Moses, and he said, 'Is there not Aaron your brother, the Levite? I know that he can speak well. And in fact he is on his way out to meet you, and when he sees you he will be glad in his heart.'
'You are to speak to him and put the words in his mouth; and I will be with your mouth and with his mouth, and I will teach you both what you are to do.'
'He will speak for you to the people; he will become a mouth for you, and you will become like God to him.'
'And take this staff in your hand; with it you are to do the signs.'
Moses went and returned to Jether his father-in-law and said to him, 'Let me go and return to my brothers in Egypt, and see whether they are still alive.' And Jethro said to Moses, 'Go in peace.'
The LORD said to Moses in Midian, 'Go, return to Egypt, for all the men who sought your life have died.'
So Moses took his wife and his sons, set them on the donkey, and returned to the land of Egypt; and Moses took the staff of God in his hand.
The LORD said to Moses, 'When you go back to Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the wonders I have put in your hand. But I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go.'
'And you are to say to Pharaoh, "This is what the LORD says: Israel is my son, my firstborn."'
'And I said to you, "Let my son go, so that he may serve me" — and you refused to let him go. So I am about to kill your son, your firstborn.'
On the way, at the place where they lodged, the LORD met him and sought to kill him.
Then Zipporah took a flint, cut off her son's foreskin, and touched it to his feet; and she said, 'Truly you are a bridegroom of blood to me.'
So he withdrew from him. It was then that she said, 'A bridegroom of blood,' because of the circumcision.
The LORD said to Aaron, 'Go into the wilderness to meet Moses.' So he went, and he met him at the mountain of God, and he kissed him.
Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD with which he had sent him, and all the signs he had commanded him to do.
Then Moses and Aaron went and gathered all the elders of the Israelites.
Aaron spoke all the words that the LORD had spoken to Moses, and he did the signs in the sight of the people.
And the people believed. When they heard that the LORD had attended to the Israelites and had seen their affliction, they bowed low and prostrated themselves.

exodus_5.t: Afterwards Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, 'This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: Let my people go, so that they may hold a festival to me in the wilderness.'
But Pharaoh said, 'Who is the LORD, that I should listen to his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go either.'
They said, 'The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God, or he may fall upon us with pestilence or with the sword.'
But the king of Egypt said to them, 'Moses and Aaron, why are you drawing the people away from their work? Get to your forced labour.'
And Pharaoh said, 'Look, the people of the land are now many, and you would make them stop their forced labour.'
That same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters over the people and their foremen:
'You are no longer to give the people straw for making bricks as you did before. Let them go and gather straw for themselves.'
'But the quota of bricks they were making before, you are to impose on them; do not reduce it. They are idle — that is why they are crying out, "Let us go and sacrifice to our God."'
'Let the labour be made heavy on the men, so that they work at it and pay no attention to lying words.'
So the taskmasters of the people and their foremen went out and said to the people, 'This is what Pharaoh says: I am not giving you straw.'
'You go and get straw for yourselves wherever you can find it — but nothing at all is reduced from your labour.'
So the people scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.
The taskmasters kept pressing them: 'Finish your work — each day's portion on its day — just as when there was straw.'

And the foremen of the Israelites, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over them, were beaten. They were asked, 'Why have you not completed your prescribed portion of brickmaking as before — yesterday and today alike?'
Then the foremen of the Israelites came and cried out to Pharaoh: 'Why do you treat your servants like this?'
'No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, "Make bricks!" And look — your servants are being beaten; and the fault is your own people's.'
But he said, 'You are idle — idle! That is why you keep saying, "Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD."'
'Now go and work. No straw will be given you, and you will still deliver the full measure of bricks.'
The foremen of the Israelites saw that they were in trouble when they were told, 'You are not to reduce your daily quota of bricks, each day's portion on its day.'
As they came out from Pharaoh, they met Moses and Aaron, who were standing there to meet them.
They said to them, 'May the LORD look upon you and judge you — you have made us a stench in the eyes of Pharaoh and of his servants, putting a sword in their hand to kill us.'
Then Moses returned to the LORD and said, 'My Lord, why have you brought harm on this people? Why did you ever send me?'
'From the time I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has brought harm on this people — and you have certainly not delivered your people.'

exodus_6.t: The LORD said to Moses, 'Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh: under a strong hand he will let them go, and under a strong hand he will drive them out of his land.'
God spoke to Moses and said to him, 'I am the LORD.'
'I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty; but by my name, the LORD, I did not make myself known to them.'
'I also established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land where they lived as sojourners.'
'And I have also heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians are making serve, and I have remembered my covenant.'

'Therefore say to the Israelites: I am the LORD. I will bring you out from under the burdens of Egypt, I will deliver you from their labour, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgement.'
'I will take you to myself as a people, and I will be God for you; and you will know that I am the LORD your God, who brings you out from under the burdens of Egypt.'
'And I will bring you into the land that I swore with uplifted hand to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob; and I will give it to you as a possession. I am the LORD.'
Moses spoke this to the Israelites, but they did not listen to Moses, out of shortness of spirit and hard labour.
Then the LORD spoke to Moses:
'Go in and speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt, that he may let the Israelites go out of his land.'
But Moses spoke before the LORD: 'Look — the Israelites have not listened to me. How then will Pharaoh listen to me, since I am uncircumcised of lips?'
But the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron and gave them a command concerning the Israelites and concerning Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.
These are the heads of their fathers' houses. The sons of Reuben, Israel's firstborn: Hanoch and Pallu, Hezron and Carmi. These are the clans of Reuben.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jakin, and Zohar, and Shaul the son of the Canaanite woman. These are the clans of Simeon.
These are the names of the sons of Levi by their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The years of Levi's life were a hundred and thirty-seven.
The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, by their clans.
The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. The years of Kohath's life were a hundred and thirty-three.
The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites by their generations.
Amram took Jochebed his father's sister as his wife, and she bore him Aaron and Moses. The years of Amram's life were a hundred and thirty-seven.
The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zikri.
The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.
Aaron took Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, as his wife, and she bore him Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.
The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These are the clans of the Korahites.
Eleazar the son of Aaron took one of the daughters of Putiel as his wife, and she bore him Phinehas. These are the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites by their clans.
That is the Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said, 'Bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt by their hosts.'
They are the ones who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt to bring the Israelites out of Egypt. That is Moses and Aaron.
On the day the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,
the LORD spoke to Moses: 'I am the LORD. Speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt everything that I speak to you.'
But Moses said before the LORD, 'Look — I am uncircumcised of lips. How will Pharaoh listen to me?'

exodus_7.t: The LORD said to Moses, "See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother will be your prophet."
You are to speak everything I command you, and Aaron your brother is to speak to Pharaoh, so that he lets the people of Israel go out of his land.
But I myself will harden Pharaoh's heart, and I will multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh will not listen to you, and I will set my hand against Egypt, and I will bring out my hosts — my people, the people of Israel — from the land of Egypt with great acts of judgement.
And the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD when I stretch out my hand over Egypt and bring the people of Israel out from among them.
Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD commanded them; so they did.
Moses was eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three years old when they spoke to Pharaoh.
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron:
"When Pharaoh says to you, 'Produce a wonder for yourselves,' then say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and throw it down before Pharaoh' — and let it become a dragon."
So Moses and Aaron came to Pharaoh and did just as the LORD had commanded. Aaron threw down his staff before Pharaoh and before his servants, and it became a dragon.
Then Pharaoh also summoned the wise men and the sorcerers, and they too — the ritual experts of Egypt — did the same by their secret arts.
Each one threw down his staff, and they became dragons; and Aaron's staff swallowed their staffs.
But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is hard; he has refused to let the people go."
Go to Pharaoh in the morning — he goes out to the water — and stand waiting to meet him on the bank of the Nile. And take in your hand the staff that was turned into a serpent.
Say to him, "The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you with this word: Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness. And look — you have not listened until now."
This is what the LORD says: By this you will know that I am the LORD. I am about to strike the waters that are in the Nile with the staff that is in my hand, and they will be turned to blood.
The fish in the Nile will die, and the Nile will stink, and the Egyptians will grow weary of drinking water from the Nile.

The LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt — over their rivers, over their canals, over their ponds, and over every pool of their waters — and they will become blood. There will be blood in all the land of Egypt, even in vessels of wood and vessels of stone.'"

Moses and Aaron did so, just as the LORD had commanded. He raised the staff and struck the waters that were in the Nile before the eyes of Pharaoh and before the eyes of his servants, and all the waters in the Nile were turned to blood.
The fish in the Nile died, and the Nile stank, and the Egyptians were not able to drink water from the Nile. There was blood in all the land of Egypt.
But the ritual experts of Egypt did the same by their secret arts; and Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he did not take even this to heart.
And all the Egyptians dug around the Nile for water to drink, because they were not able to drink from the waters of the Nile.
Seven days were completed after the LORD struck the Nile.

exodus_8.t: The LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and say to him, 'This is what the LORD says: Let my people go, that they may serve me.'"
But if you refuse to let them go, I am about to strike down your whole territory with frogs.

The Nile will swarm with frogs, and they will come up and go into your house, into your bedchamber and onto your bed, into the house of your servants and among your people, into your ovens and into your kneading troughs.
The frogs will come up on you and on your people and on all your servants.
The LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, over the canals and over the ponds, and bring the frogs up onto the land of Egypt.'"
Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt.
But the ritual experts did the same by their secret arts, and they brought frogs up onto the land of Egypt.
Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, "Plead with the LORD to remove the frogs from me and from my people, and I will let the people go, that they may sacrifice to the LORD."

Moses said to Pharaoh, "Take the honour over me: for when shall I plead for you and for your servants and for your people, that the frogs may be cut off from you and from your houses? Only in the Nile will they remain."
He said, "Tomorrow." And Moses said, "According to your word — so that you may know that there is none like the LORD our God."
The frogs will depart from you and from your houses and from your servants and from your people; only in the Nile will they remain.
Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried out to the LORD about the matter of the frogs that he had set upon Pharaoh.
The LORD did according to the word of Moses, and the frogs died out of the houses, out of the courtyards and out of the fields.
They piled them up in heap after heap, and the land stank.
But when Pharaoh saw that there was relief, he hardened his heart, and he did not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
The LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, and it will become gnats in all the land of Egypt.'"

They did so. Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and the gnats were on humankind and on livestock. All the dust of the earth became gnats in all the land of Egypt.
The ritual experts did the same by their secret arts, to bring forth the gnats, but they were not able. And the gnats were on humankind and on livestock.
The ritual experts said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.

The LORD said to Moses, "Rise early in the morning and present yourself before Pharaoh — he goes out to the water — and say to him, 'This is what the LORD says: Let my people go, that they may serve me.'"

For if you will not let my people go, I am about to send the swarm upon you and upon your servants and upon your people and into your houses. The houses of Egypt will be filled with the swarm, and also the ground on which they stand.
But on that day I will distinguish the land of Goshen, where my people are standing, so that no swarm will be there — so that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the land.
I will set a division between my people and your people. Tomorrow this sign will happen.
The LORD did so, and a heavy swarm came into the house of Pharaoh and the house of his servants; and in all the land of Egypt the land was ruined because of the swarm.
Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, "Go, sacrifice to your God in the land."

Moses said, "It is not right to do so, for we would be sacrificing to the LORD our God what Egypt finds detestable. If we sacrifice what Egypt finds detestable before their eyes, will they not stone us?"
We will go a three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God, just as he says to us.
Pharaoh said, "I will let you go, and you shall sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness; only you shall certainly not go far. Plead for me."

Moses said, "See, I am going out from you, and I will plead with the LORD, and tomorrow the swarm will depart from Pharaoh, from his servants and from his people. Only let Pharaoh not deal deceitfully again by not letting the people go to sacrifice to the LORD."
Moses went out from Pharaoh and pleaded with the LORD.
The LORD did according to the word of Moses, and he removed the swarm from Pharaoh, from his servants and from his people; not one remained.
But Pharaoh hardened his heart at this time also, and he did not let the people go.

exodus_9.t: The LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and speak to him: 'This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go, that they may serve me.'"
For if you refuse to let them go and you are still keeping a strong hold on them,
the hand of the LORD is about to fall on your livestock that are in the field — on the horses, on the donkeys, on the camels, on the cattle and on the flocks — a very heavy pestilence.
But the LORD will distinguish between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, and nothing will die of all that belongs to the people of Israel.
And the LORD set an appointed time, saying, "Tomorrow the LORD will do this thing in the land."
The LORD did this thing on the next day, and all the livestock of Egypt died; but of the livestock of the people of Israel not one died.
Pharaoh sent, and indeed, not even one of the livestock of Israel had died. But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not let the people go.
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Take handfuls of soot from a furnace, and let Moses sprinkle it toward the heavens before the eyes of Pharaoh."
It will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and on humankind and on livestock it will become boils breaking out in blisters in all the land of Egypt.
So they took the soot of the furnace and stood before Pharaoh, and Moses sprinkled it toward the heavens, and it became boils breaking out in blisters on humankind and on livestock.
The ritual experts were not able to stand before Moses because of the boils, for the boils were on the ritual experts and on all the Egyptians.
But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not listen to them, just as the LORD had said to Moses.

The LORD said to Moses, "Rise early in the morning and present yourself before Pharaoh, and say to him, 'This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go, that they may serve me.'"
For at this time I am sending all my plagues to your heart, and on your servants and on your people, so that you may know that there is none like me in all the earth.
For by now I could have stretched out my hand and struck you and your people with pestilence, and you would have been wiped out from the earth.
But for this reason I have kept you alive: to make you see my power, and so that my name may be recounted in all the earth.
You are still exalting yourself over my people by not letting them go.
At about this time tomorrow I am about to rain down very heavy hail, such as has not been in Egypt from the day it was founded until now.

And now send and bring to shelter your livestock and all that you have in the field. Every human and animal that is found in the field and not gathered into the house — the hail will come down on them and they will die.
Whoever among Pharaoh's servants feared the word of the LORD made his servants and his livestock flee into the houses.
But whoever did not take the word of the LORD to heart left his servants and his livestock in the field.

The LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward the heavens, and let there be hail in all the land of Egypt — on humankind and on livestock and on all the vegetation of the field, in the land of Egypt."
Moses stretched out his staff toward the heavens, and the LORD gave thunder and hail, and fire went to the ground; and the LORD rained hail on the land of Egypt.
There was hail, and fire flashing in the midst of the hail — very heavy, such as had not been in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation.
The hail struck everything that was in the field in all the land of Egypt, from humankind to livestock; the hail struck all the vegetation of the field, and it shattered every tree of the field.
Only in the land of Goshen, where the people of Israel were, there was no hail.
Pharaoh sent and summoned Moses and Aaron, and said to them, "I have sinned this time. The LORD is the righteous one, and I and my people are the guilty ones."
Plead with the LORD — there has been enough of God's thunder and hail — and I will let you go, and you shall not stay any longer.
Moses said to him, "As I go out of the city I will spread out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will cease and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth belongs to the LORD."
But as for you and your servants, I know that you do not yet fear before the LORD God.
The flax and the barley were struck, for the barley was in the ear and the flax was in bud.
But the wheat and the spelt were not struck, for they are late crops.
Moses went out from Pharaoh, out of the city, and spread out his hands to the LORD; and the thunder and the hail ceased, and rain was not poured out on the ground.
But when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunder had ceased, he sinned again, and he hardened his heart, he and his servants.
Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not let the people of Israel go, just as the LORD had said by the hand of Moses.

exodus_10.t: The LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh, for I myself have hardened his heart and the heart of his servants, so that I may set these signs of mine in his midst,
and so that you may recount in the hearing of your son and your son's son how I dealt ruthlessly with Egypt, and my signs that I set among them. And you will know that I am the LORD."

So Moses and Aaron came to Pharaoh and said to him, "This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go, that they may serve me.
For if you refuse to let my people go, I am about to bring locusts into your territory tomorrow.

It will cover the eye of the land, and no one will be able to see the land; and it will eat the remainder of what escaped, what is left to you from the hail, and it will eat every tree that sprouts for you from the field.

Your houses will be filled, and the houses of all your servants, and the houses of all the Egyptians — such as your fathers and your fathers' fathers have not seen from the day they were on the land until this day." Then he turned and went out from Pharaoh.
Pharaoh's servants said to him, "How long will this one be a snare to us? Let the men go, that they may serve the LORD their God. Do you not yet know that Egypt has perished?"
So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh, and he said to them, "Go, serve the LORD your God. Who and who are the ones going?"
Moses said, "With our young and with our old we will go; with our sons and with our daughters, with our flocks and with our herds we will go, for it is a festival of the LORD for us."
He said to them, "May the LORD be so with you, as I let you go and your little ones! See — you have evil in mind."
"Not so! Go, you men, and serve the LORD, for that is what you are seeking." And they were driven out from the presence of Pharaoh.
The LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, so that they may come up over the land of Egypt and eat all the vegetation of the land, all that the hail left."
So Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the LORD drove an east wind in the land all that day and all that night. When morning came, the east wind had carried the locusts.
The locusts came up over all the land of Egypt and settled in all the territory of Egypt, very heavy. Before it there had been no such locusts as it, and after it there will be none like it.

It covered the eye of all the land, and the land grew dark; and it ate all the vegetation of the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left. No greenery was left on the trees or on the vegetation of the field in all the land of Egypt.
Then Pharaoh hurried to summon Moses and Aaron, and said, "I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you."
And now, forgive my sin only this time, and plead with the LORD your God, that he may remove from me only this death.
So he went out from Pharaoh and pleaded with the LORD.
And the LORD turned a very strong sea wind, and it carried the locusts away and drove them into the Sea of Reeds. Not one locust remained in all the territory of Egypt.
But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go.
The LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward the heavens, and let there be darkness over the land of Egypt — and let the darkness be felt."
So Moses stretched out his hand toward the heavens, and there was darkness of gloom in all the land of Egypt for three days.
They did not see one another, and no one rose from where he was for three days; but for all the people of Israel there was light in their dwellings.
Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and said, "Go, serve the LORD; only your flocks and your herds shall be detained. Even your little ones may go with you."
But Moses said, "You yourself must also give into our hand sacrifices and burnt offerings, and we will offer them to the LORD our God.

And our livestock must also go with us; not a hoof shall remain, for from it we will take to serve the LORD our God. And we ourselves do not know with what we will serve the LORD until we come there."
But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he was not willing to let them go.
Pharaoh said to him, "Go from me! Take heed to yourself: do not see my face again, for on the day you see my face you will die."
Moses said, "Rightly you have spoken. I will not see your face again."

exodus_11.t: The LORD said to Moses, "Yet one affliction I will bring upon Pharaoh and upon Egypt; after that he will let you go from here. When he lets you go completely, he will certainly drive you out from here.
Speak now in the hearing of the people, and let each man ask from his neighbour and each woman from her neighbour articles of silver and articles of gold."
And the LORD gave the people favour in the eyes of the Egyptians. Also the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the eyes of Pharaoh's servants and in the eyes of the people.
Moses said, "This is what the LORD says: About the middle of the night I am going out into the midst of Egypt.
Every firstborn in the land of Egypt will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne to the firstborn of the maidservant who is behind the hand-mill, and every firstborn of livestock.
There will be a great cry in all the land of Egypt, such as has not happened and such as will not happen again.
But against all the people of Israel not a dog will bark, from human to livestock — so that you may know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.

And all these servants of yours will come down to me and bow down to me, saying, 'Go out, you and all the people who are at your feet.' And after that I will go out." Then he went out from Pharaoh in heat of anger.
The LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that my wonders may be many in the land of Egypt."
Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh; and the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go from his land.

exodus_12.t: The LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt:
This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first for you of the months of the year.
Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying: On the tenth of this month let each man take for himself a flock animal for a father's household, a flock animal for the household.

And if the household is too small for a flock animal, then he and his neighbour who is near his house shall take according to the number of persons; each according to what he eats you shall reckon for the flock animal.
The flock animal shall be unblemished, male, a year old; you shall take it from the sheep or from the goats.
And it shall be kept by you until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall slaughter it at twilight.
They shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel of the houses in which they eat it.
They shall eat the flesh in this night, roasted with fire, with unleavened bread; with bitter herbs they shall eat it.
Do not eat any of it raw, or boiled at all in water, but roasted with fire — its head with its legs and with its entrails.
You shall not leave any of it until morning; and what is left of it until morning you shall burn with fire.
And this is how you shall eat it: your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. You shall eat it in haste. It is a Passover to the LORD.

For I will pass through the land of Egypt in this night, and I will strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from humankind to livestock; and against all the gods of Egypt I will execute acts of judgement. I am the LORD.
The blood shall be for you a sign on the houses where you are; and I will see the blood and pass over you, and there shall be no blow among you for destruction when I strike in the land of Egypt.
This day shall be for you a memorial, and you shall celebrate it as a festival to the LORD; throughout your generations, as a perpetual statute, you shall celebrate it.

Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day you shall remove leaven from your houses, for anyone who eats what is leavened — that person shall be cut off from Israel, from the first day until the seventh day.
On the first day there shall be a holy assembly, and on the seventh day a holy assembly for you. No work shall be done on them; only what is eaten by every person — that alone may be done by you.
You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, for on this very day I brought your hosts out from the land of Egypt; and you shall keep this day throughout your generations, a perpetual statute.
In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, in the evening, you shall eat unleavened bread, until the twenty-first day of the month in the evening.
Seven days leaven shall not be found in your houses, for anyone who eats anything leavened — that person shall be cut off from the congregation of Israel, whether a sojourner or a native of the land.
You shall eat nothing leavened; in all your dwellings you shall eat unleavened bread.
Then Moses summoned all the elders of Israel and said to them, "Draw out and take for yourselves flock animals according to your clans, and slaughter the Passover.

And you shall take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood that is in the bowl, and touch the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood that is in the bowl. And none of you shall go out from the door of his house until morning.

For the LORD will pass through to strike down Egypt, and he will see the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, and the LORD will pass over the door and will not allow the destroyer to come into your houses to strike down.
You shall keep this word as a decree for you and for your sons forever.
And when you come into the land that the LORD will give you, just as he said, you shall keep this service.
And when your children say to you, "What is this service to you?" —

then you shall say, "It is a sacrifice of Passover to the LORD, who passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt when he struck down Egypt, and he delivered our houses." And the people bowed low and bowed down.
The people of Israel went and did just as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron; so they did.

And in the middle of the night the LORD struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive who was in the house of the pit, and every firstborn of livestock.
Pharaoh rose in the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians, and there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was no house where there was not someone dead.
He summoned Moses and Aaron in the night and said, "Rise, go out from among my people, both you and the people of Israel; and go, serve the LORD as you have said.
"Take both your flocks and your herds, as you have said, and go. And bless me also."
And the Egyptians pressed strongly upon the people, to hurry them out of the land, for they said, "We are all dying."
So the people carried off their dough before it was leavened, their kneading troughs bound up in their clothes on their shoulders.
The people of Israel did according to the word of Moses, and they asked from the Egyptians articles of silver and articles of gold and clothing.
And the LORD gave the people favour in the eyes of the Egyptians, and they granted their request; and they plundered Egypt.
The people of Israel set out from Rameses toward Succoth, about six hundred thousand on foot — the men — apart from the little ones.
