They went on from Perga and arrived at Antioch in Pisidia, and on the sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down.
After the reading of the law and the prophets, the synagogue rulers sent to them, saying, 'Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it.'
Paul stood up, motioned with his hand, and said: 'Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen.
The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and lifted the people high during their stay as foreigners in the land of Egypt, and with a raised arm he led them out of it.
And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness.
And he destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan and gave them their land as an inheritance,
over about four hundred and fifty years. After that he gave them judges, until Samuel the prophet.
And then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, a man from the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.
He removed him and raised up David as their king, about whom he also testified: 'I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do everything I want.'
From this man's seed God brought to Israel a saviour, Jesus, according to promise.
Before his coming John had proclaimed in advance a baptism of a change of mind to all the people of Israel.
As John was finishing his course he kept saying, 'What do you suppose me to be? I am not the one. But look, there is one coming after me whose sandal I am not worthy to untie.'
Brothers, sons of Abraham's family, and those among you who fear God: it is to us that the message of this rescue has been sent.
For those living in Jerusalem and their rulers did not recognise him, and by judging him they fulfilled the words of the prophets that are read every sabbath.
And though they found no ground for a death sentence, they asked Pilate to have him executed.
When they had finished everything written about him, they took him down from the tree and put him in a tomb.
But God raised him from the dead,
and for many days he was seen by those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people.
And we bring you the good news that the promise made to the fathers
God has fulfilled for us their children by raising Jesus, as it is also written in the second psalm: 'You are my son; today I have fathered you.'
And that he raised him from the dead, never again to return to decay, he has said in this way: 'I will give you the holy and faithful things of David.'
That is why he also says in another place: 'You will not give your holy one to see decay.'
For David, after serving God's purpose in his own generation, fell asleep and was gathered to his fathers and saw decay.
But the one God raised did not see decay.
So let it be known to you, brothers, that through this man release from sins is announced to you;
and from everything you could not be freed from by the law of Moses — in this one everyone who believes is freed.
So watch out that what is said in the prophets does not come upon you:
'Look, you scoffers, and be amazed, and vanish — because I am doing a work in your days, a work you will never believe even if someone tells it to you in full.'
As they were going out of the synagogue of the Jews, the nations kept urging that these things be spoken to them on the next sabbath.
When the gathering broke up, many of the Jews and of the devout proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas, who talked with them and urged them to stay with the grace of God.
On the following sabbath nearly the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.
When the Jews saw the crowds they were filled with jealousy, and they contradicted what Paul was saying, contradicting and slandering.

Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly: 'It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first. Since you push it away and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life — look, we are turning to the nations.
For this is what the Lord has commanded us: 'I have set you as a light of nations, that you may be for rescue to the end of the earth.'
When the nations heard this they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed.
And the word of the Lord was carried through the whole region.
But the Jews stirred up the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, and they raised a persecution against Paul and Barnabas and threw them out of their district.
So they shook the dust off their feet against them and went to Iconium.
And the disciples were being filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

acts_14.t: In Iconium the same thing happened: they went into the synagogue of the Jews and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed.
But the Jews who refused to be persuaded stirred up the minds of the nations and made them hostile against the brothers and sisters.
So they spent a good while there speaking openly, relying on the Lord, who testified to the message of his grace and granted signs and wonders to happen through their hands.
The city's population was split: some were with the Jews, some with the apostles.
When there was a move by both the nations and the Jews, along with their rulers, to mistreat them and stone them,
they realised it and fled to the Lycaonian cities, Lystra and Derbe and the surrounding country,
and there they went on announcing the good news.
In Lystra a man was sitting who had no power in his feet: he had been lame from his mother's womb and had never walked.
This man listened to Paul speaking. Paul looked straight at him and saw that he had trust to be made well,
and said in a loud voice, 'Stand up straight on your feet.' And he jumped up and was walking about.
When the crowds saw what Paul had done they raised their voices, saying in Lycaonian, 'The gods have come down to us in human form!'
They called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, since he was the one who led the speaking.
And the priest of the Zeus whose temple stood in front of the city brought bulls and garlands to the gates, and with the crowds he wanted to sacrifice.
When the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their clothes and rushed out into the crowd, shouting

and saying, 'Men, why are you doing this? We too are human beings with the same nature as you, and we are bringing you good news, to turn you from these empty things to the living God who made the sky and the earth and the sea and everything in them.
In the generations that have passed he let all the nations go their own ways,
and yet he did not leave himself without a witness: doing good, giving you rain from the sky and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.'
Even saying this, they barely stopped the crowds from sacrificing to them.
But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having won over the crowds they stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, thinking he was dead.
But when the disciples had gathered round him he got up and went into the city, and the next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe.
They announced the good news in that city and made a good number of disciples, and then went back to Lystra and Iconium and Antioch,
strengthening the disciples and urging them to stay in the faith, and saying that we must go through many pressures to enter the kingdom of God.
They appointed elders for them in each community, and with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had come to believe.
They passed through Pisidia and came into Pamphylia,
and after speaking the message in Perga they went down to Attalia.
From there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been handed over to the grace of God for the work they had now completed.
When they arrived they gathered the community together and reported everything God had done with them, and that he had opened a door of trust to the nations.
And they stayed there with the disciples no little time.

acts_15.t: Some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers and sisters, 'Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.'

There was no small dissension and dispute between Paul and Barnabas and them, so they arranged for Paul and Barnabas and some others of their number to go up to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem about this question.

So they were sent on their way by the community, and they passed through Phoenicia and Samaria describing in detail the turning of the nations, and they brought great joy to all the brothers and sisters.
When they arrived in Jerusalem they were welcomed by the community and the apostles and the elders, and they reported everything God had done with them.
But some believers from the party of the Pharisees stood up and said that they must be circumcised and be told to keep the law of Moses.
The apostles and the elders gathered to look into this matter.

After much dispute Peter stood up and said to them, 'Brothers, you know that in the early days God chose among you that through my mouth the nations should hear the message of the good news and believe.
And God, who knows the heart, testified for them by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us,
and he made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by trust.
So now, why are you testing God by putting a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have had the strength to carry?
No — we believe we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, in the same way as they are.'
The whole gathering went quiet, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul describing all the signs and wonders God had done through them among the nations.
After they finished, James answered: 'Brothers, listen to me.
Simeon has described how God first visited the nations to take from them a people for his name.
And the words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written:
'After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David; I will rebuild its ruins and set it upright again,
so that the rest of humanity may seek out the Lord, and all the nations on whom my name has been called, says the Lord who does these things,
known from of old.'
So my judgement is that we should not trouble those of the nations who are turning to God,
but write to them to keep away from things polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood.
For from ancient generations Moses has had those who proclaim him in every city, being read aloud in the synagogues every sabbath.'

Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole community, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, leading men among the brothers and sisters,
writing by their hand: 'The apostles and the elders, brothers, to the brothers and sisters from the nations throughout Antioch and Syria and Cilicia: greetings.
Since we have heard that some of our number went out and unsettled you with words, upsetting your minds — though we gave them no such instructions —
it seemed good to us, having come to one mind, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have handed over their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
So we have sent Judas and Silas, and they will report the same things by word of mouth.
For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these necessary things:
to keep away from things sacrificed to idols and from blood and from what is strangled and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.
So they were sent off and went down to Antioch, and they gathered the crowd together and delivered the letter.
When they read it they rejoiced at the encouragement.
Judas and Silas, being prophets themselves, encouraged the brothers and sisters with a long message and strengthened them.
After spending some time there they were sent off in peace by the brothers and sisters to those who had sent them.
[But it seemed good to Silas to stay on there.]
Paul and Barnabas stayed on in Antioch, teaching and announcing the good news of the word of the Lord, along with many others.
After some days Paul said to Barnabas, 'Let us go back and visit the brothers and sisters in every city where we announced the word of the Lord, and see how they are.'
Barnabas wanted to take John called Mark along with them,
but Paul thought it right not to take along someone who had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work.
There was a sharp clash, so that they separated from each other, and Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus.
Paul chose Silas and went out, having been handed over by the brothers and sisters to the grace of the Lord.
He travelled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the communities.

acts_16.t: He came down to Derbe and to Lystra. And there was a disciple there named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman, but of a Greek father.
The brothers and sisters in Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him.
Paul wanted this man to go out with him, so he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.
As they travelled through the cities they handed on to them the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, for them to keep.
So the communities were being strengthened in the faith and were growing in number every day.
They went through the Phrygian and Galatian region, having been prevented by the Holy Spirit from speaking the message in Asia.
When they came opposite Mysia they tried to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit of Jesus would not let them.
So they passed by Mysia and came down to Troas.
And a vision appeared to Paul during the night: a Macedonian man was standing and urging him, saying, 'Cross over into Macedonia and help us.'
When he had seen the vision, we immediately looked for a way to go out into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to announce the good news to them.
So we put to sea from Troas and ran a straight course to Samothrace, and the next day to Neapolis,
and from there to Philippi, which is a city of the first district of Macedonia, a colony. We stayed in this city some days.
On the sabbath day we went outside the gate beside a river, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had gathered.
And a woman named Lydia was listening, a dealer in purple from the city of Thyatira, a worshipper of God, whose heart the Lord opened to pay attention to what Paul was saying.
When she and her household were baptised, she urged us, saying, 'If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.' And she pressed us into it.
As we were going to the place of prayer, a slave girl met us who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners a great deal of money by telling fortunes.
She kept following Paul and us, crying out, 'These men are servants of the Most High God, who are announcing to you a way of rescue.'
She did this for many days. Paul, worn down by it, turned and said to the spirit, 'I order you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.' And it came out that very hour.
When her owners saw that their hope of profit had gone out, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers.
They brought them to the magistrates and said, 'These men are throwing our city into confusion. They are Jews,
and they are announcing customs that it is not lawful for us to accept or practise, since we are Romans.'
The crowd joined in the attack against them, and the magistrates tore their clothes off them and ordered them to be beaten with rods.
After laying many blows on them they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them securely.
Having received such an order, he threw them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. At once all the doors were opened and everyone's chains came loose.
The jailer woke up, and seeing the prison doors open he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul called out in a loud voice, 'Do yourself no harm — we are all here.'
He called for lights and rushed in, and trembling he fell down before Paul and Silas.
He brought them outside and said, 'Sirs, what must I do to be saved?'
They said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.'
And they spoke the word of the Lord to him, together with everyone in his house.
He took them at that hour of the night and washed their wounds, and he and all his household were baptised at once.
He brought them up into his house and set a table before them, and he rejoiced with his whole household that he had come to believe in God.
When day came the magistrates sent the rod-bearers with the message, 'Release those men.'
The jailer reported these words to Paul: 'The magistrates have sent word that you are to be released. So come out now and go in peace.'

But Paul said to them, 'They beat us publicly without a trial, men who are Roman citizens, and they threw us into prison — and now they are throwing us out secretly? No. Let them come themselves and bring us out.'
The rod-bearers reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Romans.
They came and appealed to them, and after bringing them out they asked them to leave the city.
So they went out of the prison and went to Lydia's house, and when they had seen the brothers and sisters they encouraged them and left.

acts_17.t: They travelled through Amphipolis and Apollonia and came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews.
As was his custom, Paul went in to them, and for three sabbaths he argued with them from the scriptures,
opening them up and setting out that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead, and that 'this Jesus, whom I announce to you, is the Christ.'
Some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, along with a great number of the devout Greeks and quite a few of the leading women.

But the Jews became jealous, and taking along some worthless men from the marketplace they formed a mob and set the city in an uproar. They attacked Jason's house, looking to bring them out to the assembly.
When they did not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers and sisters before the city officials, shouting, 'These men who have turned the world upside down have come here too,
and Jason has taken them in. All of them act against the decrees of Caesar, saying there is another king, Jesus.'
They stirred up the crowd and the city officials, who heard these things,
and after taking a security payment from Jason and the rest, they released them.
The brothers and sisters immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the synagogue of the Jews.
These were more open-minded than those in Thessalonica: they received the message with all eagerness, examining the scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.
So many of them believed, and not a few of the Greek women of high standing, and men.
But when the Jews from Thessalonica found out that the word of God had been announced by Paul in Berea as well, they came there too, shaking up and stirring the crowds.
Then the brothers and sisters immediately sent Paul off to go as far as the sea, while Silas and Timothy stayed on there.
Those escorting Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving an instruction for Silas and Timothy to come to him as quickly as possible, they left.
While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw the city full of idols.
So he argued in the synagogue with the Jews and with those who worshipped God, and in the marketplace every day with whoever happened to be there.

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debated with him. Some said, 'What is this seed-picker trying to say?' Others said, 'He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign divinities' — because he was announcing the good news of Jesus and the resurrection.
They took hold of him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, 'Can we know what this new teaching being spoken by you is?
For you are bringing some strange things to our ears, so we want to know what these things mean.'
Now all the Athenians and the foreigners staying there spent their time on nothing else than telling or hearing something newer.
Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus and said: 'Men of Athens, I see that you are in every way very religious.

For as I was going through and looking carefully at the objects of your worship, I even found an altar on which was inscribed: To an unknown god. What you worship without knowing, this I announce to you.
The God who made the world and everything in it, this one, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by hands,
and he is not served by human hands as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all life and breath and everything.
And from one man he made every nation of humanity to live on the whole face of the earth, marking out appointed seasons and the boundaries of where they live,
so that they would seek God — if perhaps they might grope after him and find him — though he is not far from each one of us.
For in him we live and move and exist, as some of your own poets have said: 'For we are also his offspring.'
So being God's offspring, we ought not to think that the divine is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by human skill and imagination.
So God overlooked the times of ignorance, and now he announces to people that everyone everywhere is to change their mind,
because he has set a day on which he is going to judge the inhabited world in rightness, by a man he has marked out — and he has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead.'
When they heard about a resurrection of the dead, some sneered, but others said, 'We will hear you about this again.'
So Paul went out from among them.
But some men joined him and believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.

acts_18.t: After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth.
He found a Jew named Aquila, a Pontian by birth, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome, and he went to them.
And because they had the same trade he stayed with them and worked; by trade they were tentmakers.
He argued in the synagogue every sabbath and tried to persuade both Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul was taken up with the message, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ.
When they set themselves against him and slandered him, he shook out his clothes and said to them, 'Your blood is on your own head. I am clean. From now on I will go to the nations.'
He moved on from there and went into the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshipper of God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.
Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believed in the Lord together with his whole household, and many of the Corinthians who heard believed and were baptised.
The Lord said to Paul in the night through a vision, 'Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent,
because I am with you, and nobody will attack you to harm you, because I have many people in this city.'
So he settled there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
While Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews rose up with one accord against Paul and brought him to the tribunal,
saying, 'This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.'
As Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, 'If it were some crime or wicked fraud, Jews, it would be reasonable for me to bear with you.
But if these are questions about a word and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I do not want to be a judge of such things.'
And he drove them away from the tribunal.
Then they all seized Sosthenes, the synagogue ruler, and beat him in front of the tribunal, and none of this mattered to Gallio.

Paul stayed on a good many days more, then said goodbye to the brothers and sisters and sailed for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. He had his head shaved at Cenchreae, for he was under a vow.
They came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and argued with the Jews.
When they asked him to stay for a longer time he did not agree,
but said goodbye, saying, 'I must by all means keep the coming feast in Jerusalem. I will come back to you again, God willing.' And he put to sea from Ephesus.
He landed at Caesarea, went up and greeted the community, and went down to Antioch.
After spending some time there he set out, going through the Galatian region and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples.
A Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth, an eloquent man, arrived at Ephesus. He was powerful in the scriptures.
He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in spirit he spoke and taught accurately the things about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.

When he wanted to cross over into Achaia, the brothers and sisters encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived he was a great help to those who had come to believe through grace,
for he vigorously refuted the Jews in public, showing through the scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.

acts_19.t: While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul went through the inland regions and came down to Ephesus and found some disciples.
He said to them, 'Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?' They said to him, 'No — we have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.'
He said, 'Into what then were you baptised?' They said, 'Into John's baptism.'
Paul said, 'John baptised with a baptism of a change of mind, telling the people to believe in the one coming after him, that is, in Jesus.'
When they heard this they were baptised into the name of the Lord Jesus,
and when Paul laid his hands on them the Holy Spirit came on them, and they were speaking in tongues and prophesying.
In all there were about twelve men.
He went into the synagogue and spoke boldly for three months, arguing and persuading about the kingdom of God.

But when some grew hard and refused to be persuaded, speaking evil of the Way in front of the crowd, he withdrew from them and took the disciples apart, arguing daily in the lecture hall of a man named Tyrannus.
This went on for two years, so that everyone living in Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.
God was doing works of power through Paul's hands that were not the ordinary kind,
so that even handkerchiefs and work-aprons that had touched his skin were carried to the sick, and the diseases left them and the evil spirits went out.
Some of the travelling Jewish exorcists undertook to name the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, 'I bind you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.'
There were seven sons of a Jewish chief priest named Sceva doing this.
But the evil spirit answered them, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I am acquainted with — but who are you?'
And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, overpowered them all and prevailed against them, so that they ran out of that house naked and wounded.
This became known to everyone living in Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks, and fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.
Many of those who had believed came confessing and disclosing what they had been doing.

And a good number of those who had practised magic arts brought their books together and burned them in front of everyone. They added up the prices and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver.
So the word of the Lord kept growing and prevailing mightily.
When these things were completed, Paul resolved in the spirit to go to Jerusalem, passing through Macedonia and Achaia, saying, 'After I have been there, I must see Rome too.'
He sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, into Macedonia, while he himself stayed on for a while in Asia.
About that time there was no small disturbance about the Way.
For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no small business to the craftsmen.
He gathered them together, with the workers in similar trades, and said, 'Men, you know that our prosperity comes from this business,
and you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a sizeable crowd, saying that gods made by hands are not gods.

And there is a danger not only that this line of ours will fall into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing, and that she will be brought down from her magnificence — she whom the whole of Asia and the inhabited world worships.'
When they heard this they were filled with rage and kept shouting, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'
The city was filled with confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theatre, dragging along Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul's travelling companions.
Paul wanted to go in to the assembled people, but the disciples would not let him.
Some of the Asiarchs too, who were his friends, sent to him and urged him not to venture into the theatre.
So some were shouting one thing and some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together.
Some of the crowd instructed Alexander, whom the Jews had pushed forward. Alexander motioned with his hand and wanted to make a defence to the people.
But when they recognised that he was a Jew, one voice went up from them all for about two hours, shouting, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'

The city secretary quietened the crowd and says, 'Men of Ephesus, what person is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple-keeper of the great Artemis and of the image that fell from the sky?
Since these things cannot be contradicted, you ought to be calm and do nothing rash.
For you brought these men here, and they are neither temple-robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.
So if Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a case against anyone, court days are held and there are proconsuls: let them bring charges against each other.
And if you are looking for anything further, it will be settled in the lawful assembly.
For we are in danger of being charged with rioting over today, since there is no cause we will be able to give an account for concerning this gathering.
And when he had said this, he dismissed the assembly.

acts_20.t: After the uproar had died down, Paul sent for the disciples, encouraged them, said his goodbyes, and left to travel to Macedonia.
He travelled through those regions, encouraging the people there at length, and came into Greece.
He spent three months there, and when a plot was formed against him by the Jews just as he was about to put out to sea for Syria, he decided to go back by way of Macedonia.
Sopater son of Pyrrhus, from Beroea, went with him as far as Asia, and from the Thessalonians Aristarchus and Secundus, and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy, and from Asia Tychicus and Trophimus.
These men went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas.
We ourselves sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we reached them at Troas, where we stayed seven days.
On the first day of the week, when we had gathered to break bread, Paul was talking with them, and since he meant to leave the next day he kept on speaking until midnight.
There were a good many lamps in the upstairs room where we had gathered.

A young man named Eutychus was sitting in the window, sinking into a deep sleep, and as Paul talked on and on he was carried under by the sleep and fell from the third storey down, and was picked up dead.
Paul went down, threw himself on him, took him in his arms and said, "Stop making a commotion — his life is in him."
Then he went back up, broke the bread and ate, and talked with them a long while, until daybreak, and then left.
They took the boy away alive, and were comforted more than a little.
We went ahead to the ship and set sail for Assos, meaning to take Paul aboard there; he had arranged it that way, intending to go on foot himself.
When he met us at Assos we took him aboard and came to Mitylene.
Sailing from there, the next day we arrived opposite Chios; the day after we crossed over to Samos and stayed at Trogyllium; and the following day we came to Miletus.
Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so that he would not have to spend time in Asia; he was in a hurry to be in Jerusalem, if he possibly could, on the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus he sent word to Ephesus and called for the elders of the community.
When they arrived he said to them: "You know for yourselves how I lived among you the whole time, from the first day I set foot in Asia —
serving the Lord as a slave serves, with all lowliness and with tears, through the trials that came to me from the plots of the Jews;
how I held back nothing that was for your good, but announced it to you and taught you, in public and from house to house,
testifying to Jews and Greeks alike about the change of mind that turns toward God, and about trust in our Lord Jesus Christ.
And now, look: bound in the spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will meet me there,
except that in city after city the Holy Spirit testifies to me that chains and hardships are waiting for me.
But I count my own life of no value to myself, if only I may finish my course and the service I received from the Lord Jesus — to testify to the good news of God's grace.
And now, look: I know that none of you, among whom I went about proclaiming the kingdom, will see my face again.
So I testify to you this very day that I am clean of the blood of everyone.
For I did not hold back from announcing to you the whole purpose of God.
Keep watch over yourselves and over the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit set you as overseers, to shepherd the community of God, which he obtained with his own blood.
I know that after I am gone savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock,
and from among your own number men will rise up and speak twisted things, to drag the disciples away after themselves.
So stay awake, remembering that for three years, night and day, I never stopped warning each one of you, with tears.
And now I entrust you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who have been made holy.
I coveted no one's silver or gold or clothing.
You know for yourselves that these hands served my own needs and the needs of the men with me.
In everything I showed you that by labouring like this we must take hold of the weak, and remember the words of the Lord Jesus — that he himself said, "It is more blessed to give than to receive."
When he had said this he knelt down with them all and prayed.
They all wept a great deal, and threw their arms around Paul's neck and kissed him,
grieving most of all over what he had said, that they would never see his face again. And they went with him down to the ship.

acts_21.t: When we had torn ourselves away from them and put out to sea, we ran a straight course and came to Cos, the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
We found a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, went aboard, and put out to sea.
We sighted Cyprus, left it behind on our left, and sailed on to Syria and put in at Tyre, because the ship was to unload its cargo there.
We looked for the disciples and found them, and stayed there seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to set foot in Jerusalem.
When our days there were up we left and went on our way, and all of them, with their wives and children, escorted us out of the city; and we knelt down on the beach and prayed
and said goodbye to one another. Then we went aboard the ship, and they went back to their own homes.
We finished the voyage from Tyre and arrived at Ptolemais, where we greeted the brothers and sisters and stayed one day with them.
The next day we left and came to Caesarea, and we went into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him.
He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.
While we were staying there for a number of days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea,

and he came to us, took Paul's belt, tied up his own feet and hands, and said, "This is what the Holy Spirit says: the man whose belt this is, the Jews in Jerusalem will tie up like this, and will hand him over into the hands of the Gentiles."
When we heard this, we and the local people begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, "What are you doing, weeping and crushing my heart? I am ready not only to be tied up but to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus."
When he would not be persuaded we fell silent and said, "Let the Lord's will be done."
After those days we got our baggage together and went up to Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea came with us too, bringing us to the man we were to lodge with — a certain Mnason of Cyprus, a disciple from the early days.
When we arrived in Jerusalem the brothers and sisters welcomed us gladly.
The next day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were there.
He greeted them and then related, one by one, the things God had done among the Gentiles through his service.
When they heard it they praised God, and they said to him, "You see, brother, how many tens of thousands there are among the Jews who have come to trust, and they are all zealous for the law.
But they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews among the Gentiles to break away from Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or to walk in the customs.
So what is to be done? A crowd is bound to gather, because they will hear that you have come.
So do what we tell you. We have four men here who are under a vow.

Take these men, be purified along with them, and pay their expenses so that they can have their heads shaved. Then everyone will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself keep in step, guarding the law.

As for the Gentiles who have come to trust, we ourselves sent a letter with our decision that they should keep themselves from what has been offered to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from sexual immorality.

Then Paul took the men, and the next day he was purified with them and went into the temple, giving notice of when the days of purification would be completed and the offering would be made for each one of them.
When the seven days were almost over, the Jews from Asia saw him in the temple, threw the whole crowd into confusion, and laid hands on him,

shouting, "Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against our people and the law and this place — and now he has even brought Greeks into the temple and defiled this holy place."
They had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian in the city with him, and they assumed Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was stirred up, the people came running together, and they seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple; and at once the doors were shut.
They were trying to kill him when a report went up to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in turmoil.
He immediately took soldiers and centurions and ran down on them; and when they saw the tribune and the soldiers they stopped beating Paul.
Then the tribune came up, arrested him, and ordered him bound with two chains, and began asking who he was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd were shouting one thing and some another; and since he could not learn anything certain because of the uproar, he ordered Paul brought into the barracks.
When he reached the steps, he had to be carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd;
for the mass of the people kept following and shouting, "Away with him!"
As he was about to be taken into the barracks Paul says to the tribune, "Am I allowed to say something to you?" He said, "You know Greek?
So you are not the Egyptian who stirred up a revolt a while back and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the desert?"
Paul said, "I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I ask you, let me speak to the people."
When he gave permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned to the people with his hand; and when a deep silence had fallen he spoke to them in the Hebrew language, saying:

acts_22.t: "Brothers and fathers, listen to the defence I am now making before you."
When they heard him addressing them in the Hebrew language they became even quieter. And he says:
"I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia but brought up in this city, trained at the feet of Gamaliel in the strictness of our ancestral law, and zealous for God, just as all of you are today.
I persecuted this Way to the death, tying up and handing over to prison both men and women,

as the high priest and the whole council of elders can testify for me. I received letters from them to the brothers in Damascus, and I was on my way to bring those who were there back to Jerusalem in chains to be punished.
As I was travelling and getting near Damascus, about midday, suddenly a great light out of heaven flashed all around me.
I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?'
I answered, 'Who are you, Lord?' And he said to me, 'I am Jesus the Nazorean, whom you are persecuting.'
The men with me saw the light, but they did not understand the voice of the one speaking to me.
I said, 'What am I to do, Lord?' And the Lord said to me, 'Get up and go into Damascus, and there you will be told about everything that has been appointed for you to do.'
Since I could not see, because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those with me and came into Damascus.
A man named Ananias, devout according to the law and well spoken of by all the Jews living there,
came to me, stood over me and said, 'Brother Saul, look up.' And in that very hour I looked up at him.
He said, 'The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, and to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his own mouth;
because you will be a witness for him to all people of what you have seen and heard.
And now, why are you waiting? Get up, be baptised, and have your sins washed away, calling on his name.'
When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance
and saw him saying to me, 'Hurry, get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.'
And I said, 'Lord, they themselves know that I was the one imprisoning and flogging those who trusted in you, synagogue by synagogue;
and when the blood of Stephen your witness was being poured out, I was standing there myself, approving, and guarding the clothes of the men who killed him.'
And he said to me, 'Go, because I am going to send you far away, to the Gentiles.'"
They listened to him up to this word, and then they raised their voices and said, "Away with such a man from the earth! It was never fit for him to live."
As they were screaming and flinging off their cloaks and throwing dust into the air,
the tribune ordered him brought into the barracks, saying that he was to be examined under the lash, so that he could find out why they were shouting at him like this.
But when they had stretched him out for the straps, Paul said to the centurion standing there, "Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman, and uncondemned?"
When the centurion heard this he went to the tribune and reported it: "Look at what you are about to do — this man is a Roman."
The tribune came and said to him, "Tell me, are you a Roman?" He said, "Yes."
The tribune answered, "I bought this citizenship for a large sum." Paul said, "But I was born into it."
So those who were about to examine him drew back from him at once; and the tribune too was afraid when he realised that he was a Roman and that he was the one who had bound him.

The next day, wanting to know for certain what he was being accused of by the Jews, he released him from his chains and ordered the chief priests and their whole council to assemble; and he brought Paul down and stood him before them.

acts_23.t: Paul looked straight at the council and said, "Brothers, I have lived my whole life before God with a completely good conscience up to this day."
The high priest Ananias ordered the men standing beside him to strike him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him, "God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit there judging me by the law, and you break the law by ordering me to be struck?"
Those standing there said, "Do you insult God's high priest?"
Paul said, "I did not know, brothers, that he is high priest; for it is written, 'You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.'"

Paul knew that one part of them were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, so he kept shouting out in the council, "Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is about a hope, and about resurrection of the dead, that I am being judged."
When he said this, a quarrel broke out between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was split.
For Sadducees say there is no resurrection, and no angel or spirit; but Pharisees acknowledge them all.

There was a great outcry, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees' party stood up and argued fiercely: "We find nothing wrong in this man. And if a spirit spoke to him, or an angel — let us not fight against God."
As the quarrel grew violent, the tribune was afraid Paul would be torn apart by them, and he ordered the troops to go down, seize him out of the middle of them, and bring him into the barracks.
The following night the Lord stood over him and said, "Take heart. As you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify in Rome as well."
When day came, the Jews formed a conspiracy and put themselves under a curse, saying they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.
There were more than forty who made this sworn plot;
they went to the chief priests and the elders and said, "We have bound ourselves under a solemn curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.
So now you, along with the council, notify the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you meant to look into his case more exactly; and we are ready to do away with him before he gets near."
But the son of Paul's sister heard about the ambush, and he came and got into the barracks and told Paul.
Paul called one of the centurions and said, "Take this young man to the tribune; he has something to report to him."
So he took him and brought him to the tribune, and says, "The prisoner Paul called me and asked me to bring this young man to you; he has something to say to you."
The tribune took him by the hand, drew him aside privately, and asked, "What is it you have to report to me?"
He said, "The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though it meant to inquire into his case more exactly.

So do not let them persuade you, because more than forty of their men are lying in wait for him, and they have put themselves under a curse neither to eat nor to drink until they have done away with him; and now they are ready, waiting for your consent."
So the tribune dismissed the young man, ordering him, "Tell no one that you have disclosed this to me."
Then he called two of the centurions and said, "Get two hundred soldiers ready to go as far as Caesarea, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen, from nine tonight,"
and to provide animals for Paul to ride, so as to bring him through safely to Felix the governor.
And he wrote a letter along these lines:
Claudius Lysias, to His Excellency Governor Felix: greetings.
This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them, when I came on them with the troops and rescued him, having learned that he is a Roman.
Wanting to know the charge on which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council.
I found that he was accused about disputed questions of their law, but had no charge against him deserving death or chains.
And when I was informed that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him. Farewell.
So the soldiers took Paul, as they had been ordered, and brought him through the night to Antipatris.
The next day they let the horsemen go on with him, and returned to the barracks.
The horsemen came into Caesarea, delivered the letter to the governor, and presented Paul to him as well.
When he had read it he asked what province he was from, and on learning that he was from Cilicia,
he said, "I will hear you fully when your accusers arrive too." And he ordered him kept under guard in Herod's praetorium.

acts_24.t: Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and an advocate named Tertullus, and they laid information against Paul before the governor.
When Paul had been called in, Tertullus began the accusation: "Since we enjoy much peace through you, and since reforms are coming to this nation through your foresight,
we welcome it in every way and everywhere, most excellent Felix, with all gratitude.
But so as not to hold you up any longer, I ask you in your fairness to give us a brief hearing.
We have found this man to be a plague, stirring up factions among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazoreans.
He even tried to profane the temple, and we seized him, and we wanted to judge him by our own law.
[But Lysias the tribune came along and, with great violence, took him out of our hands,]
He ordered his accusers to come to you. From him you will be able, by examining him yourself, to learn about everything we are accusing him of."
The Jews joined in the attack, insisting that this was so.
When the governor motioned to him to speak, Paul answered: "Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I make my defence cheerfully.
You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem.
They did not find me arguing with anyone in the temple, or gathering a crowd, in the synagogues or anywhere in the city;
and they cannot produce evidence to you for the things they are now accusing me of.
But I do admit this to you: that according to the Way — which they call a sect — I serve the God of our fathers, trusting everything laid down in the law and written in the prophets,
and I have a hope toward God — one these men themselves are waiting for — that there is going to be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust.
In this I too train myself always to keep a conscience that does not stumble, toward God and toward people.
After several years I came to bring charitable gifts to my nation, and offerings.
It was while I was doing this that they found me in the temple, purified — with no crowd and no disturbance.
But it was some Jews from Asia — and they are the ones who ought to be here before you and bring a charge, if they have anything against me.
Or let these men here say what wrong they found when I stood before the council —
unless it is this one sentence I shouted out as I stood among them: 'It is about the resurrection of the dead that I am being judged before you today.'"
Felix, who knew the facts about the Way quite exactly, adjourned them, saying, "When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will settle your case."
He instructed the centurion to keep him in custody but to give him some freedom, and not to stop any of his own people from looking after him.
Some days later Felix arrived with Drusilla, his own wife, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and listened to him about trust in Christ Jesus.
But as he discussed rightness, self-control and the judgment that is coming, Felix became frightened and answered, "That is enough for now — go. When I get an opportunity I will send for you."
At the same time he was hoping that money would be given him by Paul, so that he could release him; and so he sent for him quite often and talked with him.
When two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus; and wanting to lay up a favour with the Jews, Felix left Paul in chains.

acts_25.t: So Festus, having taken up his province, went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea three days later,
and the chief priests and the leading men of the Jews laid information before him against Paul. They kept pressing him,
asking as a favour against Paul that he would have him brought to Jerusalem — while they made an ambush to do away with him along the road.
Festus answered that Paul was being kept at Caesarea, and that he himself was about to leave shortly.
"So," he says, "let those among you who have standing come down with me, and if there is anything out of place in the man, let them accuse him."
After spending not more than eight or ten days among them, he went down to Caesarea, and the next day he sat on the judgment seat and ordered Paul to be brought in.
When he arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious charges against him which they could not prove,
while Paul made his defence: "I have committed no offence against the law of the Jews, or against the temple, or against Caesar."
But Festus, wanting to lay up a favour with the Jews, answered Paul, "Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be judged there before me on these charges?"
Paul said, "I am standing before Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged. I have done the Jews no wrong, as you yourself know perfectly well.

If I am in the wrong and have done anything deserving death, I do not ask to be spared dying. But if there is nothing in what these men accuse me of, no one can hand me over to them as a favour. I appeal to Caesar."
Then Festus conferred with his council and answered, "You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you will go."
Some days later King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and paid their respects to Festus.
Since they were staying there several days, Festus laid Paul's case before the king: "There is a man here left behind as a prisoner by Felix,
about whom, when I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid information, asking for a sentence against him.
I answered them that it is not the Roman custom to hand over any person as a favour before the accused has met his accusers face to face and been given a chance to defend himself against the charge.
So when they had come here with me, I made no delay: the next day I sat on the judgment seat and ordered the man brought in.
But when his accusers stood up they brought no charge of the sort of wickedness I had been expecting.
They had certain disputes with him about their own religion, and about a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul kept asserting was alive.
I was at a loss how to investigate such matters, so I asked whether he was willing to go to Jerusalem and be judged there about them.
But when Paul appealed to be kept for the decision of His Majesty, I ordered him kept until I could send him up to Caesar."
Agrippa said to Festus, "I would like to hear the man myself." "Tomorrow," he says, "you will hear him."
So the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the audience hall, along with the tribunes and the leading men of the city; and at Festus's order Paul was brought in.

And Festus says, "King Agrippa, and all you men present here with us: you see this man, about whom the whole crowd of the Jews petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.
But I myself found that he had done nothing deserving death; and when he appealed to His Majesty, I decided to send him.
I have nothing definite to write about him to my lord, so I have brought him before all of you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after the examination I may have something to write.
For it seems unreasonable to me to send a prisoner on without indicating the charges against him."

acts_26.t: Agrippa said to Paul, "You are permitted to speak for yourself." Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defence:
"Concerning everything I am accused of by Jews, King Agrippa, I count myself fortunate that it is before you I am to make my defence today,
especially since you are an expert in all the customs and disputed questions among Jews. So I beg you to hear me patiently.
My way of life from my youth, lived from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known to all the Jews.
They have known me from the first, and could testify if they were willing, that I lived by the strictest party of our religion — as a Pharisee.
And now I stand on trial for the hope of the promise God made to our fathers,
which our twelve tribes hope to reach as they serve God earnestly night and day. It is for this hope, King, that I am accused by the Jews.
Why is it judged unbelievable among you people that God raises the dead?
Now I myself was convinced that I had to do many things against the name of Jesus the Nazorean,
and that is what I did in Jerusalem. I shut many of the holy ones up in prisons, having received the authority from the chief priests, and when they were being put to death I cast my vote.
In synagogue after synagogue I often punished them and kept trying to force them to blaspheme, and in a raging fury against them I pursued them even to cities outside.
On that business I was travelling to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests,
when at midday along the road I saw, King, a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, blazing around me and those travelling with me.
We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.'
I said, 'Who are you, Lord?' And the Lord said, 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But get up and stand on your feet. This is why I appeared to you: to appoint you as a servant and a witness both of what you have seen of me and of what I will show you,
rescuing you from the people and from the Gentiles — to whom I am sending you

to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the authority of Satan to God, and so receive release from sins and a share among those who have been made holy by trust in me.'
So, King Agrippa, I did not disobey the heavenly vision,

but I announced, first to those in Damascus and then in Jerusalem and throughout the whole country of Judea, and to the Gentiles, that they should change their minds and turn to God, doing works worthy of that change of mind.
It was because of this that the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me with their own hands.
But I have had help from God to this very day, and so I stand here testifying to small and great alike, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen —
whether the Christ is subject to suffering, and whether, first from the resurrection of the dead, he would proclaim light to the people and to the Gentiles."
As he was making this defence, Festus says in a loud voice, "You are out of your mind, Paul! All that learning is turning you to madness."
But Paul says, "I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus. I am speaking words of truth and sober sense.
The king knows about these things, and I speak to him freely. I am not persuaded that any of this has escaped him — none of it — for it was not done in a corner.
Do you trust the prophets, King Agrippa? I know that you do."
Agrippa said to Paul, "In so short a time are you persuading me to become a Christian?"
Paul said, "I would pray to God that whether in a little or in much, not only you but all who are listening to me today might become such as I am — except for these chains."
Then the king stood up, and the governor, and Bernice, and those sitting with them;
and as they withdrew they said to one another, "This man is doing nothing that deserves death or chains."
And Agrippa said to Festus, "This man could have been released, if he had not appealed to Caesar."

acts_27.t: When it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan Cohort.
We boarded a ship of Adramyttium that was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, and put out to sea, with Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, with us.
The next day we put in at Sidon, and Julius treated Paul humanely and let him go to his friends and be looked after.
Putting out from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us,
and after sailing across the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia we came down to Myra in Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy, and put us aboard her.
For a good many days we made slow headway and barely got off Cnidus, and since the wind would not let us get on we sailed under the lee of Crete, off Salmone,
and coasting along it with difficulty we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea.
A good deal of time had been lost, and sailing was already dangerous because the Fast had already gone by, so Paul began to warn them,
saying to them, "Men, I can see that this voyage is going to end in violence and heavy loss — not only of the cargo and the ship but of our lives as well."
But the centurion was persuaded more by the helmsman and the ship's owner than by what Paul said.

Since the harbour was unsuitable for wintering, the majority decided on a plan to put out from there, in the hope of somehow reaching Phoenix — a harbour of Crete looking southwest and northwest — and wintering there.
When a south wind came up gently, they thought they had got what they wanted; they weighed anchor and began coasting along Crete, close in.
But before long a hurricane-force wind, the one called the Northeaster, came beating down off the island.
The ship was caught and could not face into the wind, so we gave way and were driven along.
Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to get the ship's boat under control.
They hoisted it aboard and then used cables to undergird the ship, frapping the hull; and fearing they would run onto the Syrtis they lowered the sea anchor, and so were carried along.
The next day, as we were being violently battered by the storm, they began throwing cargo overboard;
and on the third day they threw the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands.
For many days neither sun nor stars appeared, and no small storm lay on us, so that in the end all hope of our being saved was being stripped away.

They had gone a long time without food. Then Paul stood up among them and said, "Men, you should have listened to me and not put out from Crete; you would have gained by avoiding this violence and loss.
But now I urge you to keep your courage up. There will be no loss of life among you — only of the ship.
For last night there stood beside me an angel of the God whose I am and whom I serve,
saying, 'Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar — and look, God has granted you all those sailing with you.'
So keep up your courage, men, because I trust God that it will be exactly as it was told me.
But we must run aground on some island."
When the fourteenth night came and we were being driven across the Adriatic, about midnight the sailors began to suspect that land was coming up on them.
They took a sounding and found twenty fathoms; a little further on they sounded again and found fifteen.
Afraid that we might run onto rocky ground somewhere, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come.
The sailors were trying to escape from the ship, and they lowered the ship's boat into the sea on the pretext of laying out anchors from the bow.
Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, "Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved."
So the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship's boat and let it fall away.
Just before daybreak Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, "Today is the fourteenth day you have gone on waiting, without food, taking nothing.
So I urge you to take some food; this is for your survival. Not a hair will be lost from the head of any of you."
When he had said this he took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, broke it, and began to eat.
They all took heart and took some food themselves.
In all there were two hundred and seventy-six of us on the ship.
When they had eaten enough they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea.
When day came they did not recognise the land, but they made out a bay with a beach, and they planned to drive the ship onto it if they could.
They cut away the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosing the lashings of the steering-oars; then they hoisted the foresail to the wind and made for the beach.
But they struck a place where two seas met and ran the ship aground. The bow stuck fast and stayed immovable, while the stern began to break up under the force of the waves.
The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, so that none of them would swim away and escape.
But the centurion, wanting to bring Paul through safely, stopped them from carrying out the plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land,
and the rest to follow, some on planks and some on pieces of the ship. And so it came about that they all came safely through to land.

acts_28.t: Once we were safely through, we then found out that the island was called Malta.
The local people showed us extraordinary kindness: they lit a fire and welcomed us all, because rain had set in and it was cold.
Paul had gathered a bundle of brushwood and was putting it on the fire when a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand.
When the local people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, "This man is certainly a murderer: he came safely through the sea, but Justice has not let him live."
But he shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm.
They were expecting him to swell up or suddenly drop dead; but after waiting a long time and seeing nothing out of the ordinary happen to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god.
In the neighbourhood of that place were lands belonging to the leading man of the island, named Publius, who took us in and entertained us hospitably for three days.
It happened that Publius's father was in bed, ill with recurring fever and dysentery; Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hands on him and healed him.
After this happened, the rest of the people on the island who had illnesses came and were cured.
They honoured us with many honours, and when we were putting out to sea they put on board what we needed.
After three months we put to sea in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered at the island, with the Twin Brothers as its figurehead.
We put in at Syracuse and stayed three days,
and from there we cast off and arrived at Rhegium. After one day a south wind came up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli,
where we found brothers and sisters and were urged to stay with them seven days. And so we came to Rome.
The brothers and sisters there heard about us and came to meet us as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns; when Paul saw them he thanked God and took courage.
When we came into Rome, the centurion handed the prisoners over to the commander of the camp; but Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who was guarding him.

Three days later he called together the leading men of the Jews; and when they had come together he said to them, "Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, I was handed over as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans.
They examined me and wanted to release me, because there was no ground for a death sentence in my case.
But when the Jews objected, I was forced to appeal to Caesar — not that I had any charge to bring against my own nation.
That is why I asked to see you and speak with you; for it is because of the hope of Israel that I have this chain around me."
They said to him, "We have received no letters about you from Judea, and none of the brothers who have arrived has reported or said anything bad about you.
But we think it right to hear from you what you think, since as for this sect, we know that it is spoken against everywhere."

They arranged a day with him and came to him at his lodging in even greater numbers; and he laid it out for them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to persuade them about Jesus, from the law of Moses and from the prophets, from morning until evening.
Some were persuaded by what was said; others did not believe.
They disagreed among themselves and began to leave, after Paul had said one thing: "The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet to your fathers,
saying: 'Go to this people and say: You will hear and hear, and never understand; you will look and look, and never see.

For this people's heart has grown thick, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and their eyes they have shut — so that they might not see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I will heal them.'
So let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they too will listen."
[And when he had said this, the Jews went away, having a great dispute among themselves.]
He stayed two whole years in his own rented lodging, and welcomed everyone who came in to him,
proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with complete boldness — unhindered.

colossians_1.t: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through God's will, and Timothy our brother,
to God's people in Colossae, the faithful brothers and sisters in Christ: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,
since we heard of your trust in Christ Jesus and of the love you have for all God's people,
because of the hope stored up for you in the heavens, which you heard about beforehand in the word of the truth of the good news
which has come to you, just as in all the world it is bearing fruit and growing — as it has among you also, from the day you heard and came to know God's grace in truth.
just as you learned it from Epaphras, our beloved fellow slave, who is a faithful servant of Christ on your behalf,
and he is the one who told us about your love in the Spirit.
For this reason we too, from the day we heard, have not stopped praying for you and asking that you be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding,
so that you may walk worthily of the Lord, fully pleasing him, bearing fruit in every good work and growing in the knowledge of God,
being strengthened with all power according to the might of his glory, for all endurance and patience — with joy
giving thanks to the Father, who made you fit for a share in the allotted portion of God's people in the light;
He rescued us from the authority of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son he loves,
in whom we have release, the forgiveness of sins.
He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation;

because in him all things were created — those in the heavens and those on the earth, the visible and the invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things have been created through him and for him.
And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.
And he is the head of the body, the community; he is the beginning, the firstborn from among the dead, so that he himself might come to be first in all things.
because God was pleased to have all the fullness dwell in him,
and through him to reconcile all things to himself, having made peace through the blood of his cross — through him, whether the things on the earth or the things in the heavens.
And you, who were once estranged and hostile in mind, engaged in evil deeds —
But now he has reconciled you in the body of his flesh, through death, to present you holy, unblemished and free of accusation before him.
— if indeed you continue in the faith, founded and firm, not shifting from the hope of the good news you heard, which was proclaimed in all creation under heaven, of which I, Paul, became a servant.
Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I fill up in turn what is lacking of the afflictions of Christ, for the sake of his body, which is the community;
of which I became a servant, according to the stewardship from God that was given me for you, to fulfil the word of God —
the mystery hidden from the ages and from the generations, but now made visible to his people.
To them God chose to make known what the riches of the glory of this mystery among the nations is — which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
It is he whom we announce, warning every person and teaching every person in all wisdom, so that we may present every person complete in Christ Jesus.
For this I labour, struggling according to his working, which works powerfully in me.

colossians_2.t: I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those in Laodicea, and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh,
so that their hearts may be encouraged, knit together in love and brought to all the riches of full assurance of understanding, to the knowledge of God's mystery — of the Father and of Christ —
in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden away.
I say this so that no one may deceive you with persuasive argument.
For even if I am absent in the flesh, I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the solid front of your trust in Christ.
So then, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him,
rooted and being built up in him, and made firm in the faith just as you were taught, overflowing in it with thanksgiving.
See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, following human tradition, following the elemental spirits of the world and not Christ.
because in him all the fullness of deity dwells bodily,
and you have been filled in him, who is the head of every ruler and authority.
In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the stripping off of the body of the sins of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ,
having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through trust in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.
And you, who were dead in your trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses.
He wiped out the handwritten note of debt that stood against us with its decrees — the one that was opposed to us — and he has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.
Having stripped the rulers and authorities, he made a public example of them, leading them in a triumphal procession in him.
So do not let anyone judge you in matters of food and drink, or in the matter of a festival or a new moon or sabbaths.
These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body belongs to Christ.
Let no one disqualify you, delighting in self-abasement and the worship of angels, taking his stand on things he has seen, puffed up for no reason by the mind of his flesh,
and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, supplied and held together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that comes from God.
If you died with Christ to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as though you were still living in the world, do you submit to decrees:
'Do not handle! Do not taste! Do not touch!'
— all of which are destined to perish with use — following human commands and teachings.
These things have a reputation for wisdom, with their self-made religion and self-abasement and severity to the body, but they are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh.

colossians_3.t: So if you were raised with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is, seated at God's right hand.
Set your minds on the things above, not on the things on the earth.
For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
When Christ — your life — is made visible, then you also will be made visible with him in glory.
So put to death what belongs to the earth in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed, which is idolatry.
Because of these, God's anger is coming on the sons of disobedience.
You too once walked in these ways, when you were living in them.
But now you also must put all these away: anger, rage, malice, slander, filthy talk out of your mouth.
Do not lie to one another, since you have stripped off the old person with its practices
and have put on the new, which is being renewed toward knowledge according to the image of the one who created it.
Here there is no Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free — but Christ is all and in all.
So put on, as God's chosen ones, holy and loved: a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience —
bearing with one another and forgiving each other, if anyone has a complaint against another. Just as the Lord forgave you, so also you must forgive.
And over all these, put on love, which is the bond of completeness.
And let the peace of Christ act as umpire in your hearts, to which you were also called in one body. And be thankful.
Let the word of Christ live among you richly, in all wisdom, as you teach and warn one another with psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to God.
And whatever you do in word or in deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
Wives, submit to your own husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
Husbands, love your wives and do not become harsh toward them.
Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing in the Lord.
Fathers, do not provoke your children, so that they do not lose heart.
Slaves, obey your masters according to the flesh in everything — not with eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with singleness of heart, fearing the Lord.
Whatever you do, work at it from the soul, as for the Lord and not for people,
knowing that from the Lord you will receive the repayment of the inheritance. You serve the Lord Christ as slaves.
For the one who does wrong will be paid back for the wrong he did, and there is no favouritism.

colossians_4.t: Masters, provide your slaves with what is just and fair, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven.
Devote yourselves to prayer, staying alert in it with thanksgiving,
praying at the same time for us too, that God may open a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ — for which I am in chains —
so that I may make it visible, as I must speak.
